formal.estimand:
Three different quantities are being called "hierarchy" or "brand effect". Index persons i, months t, cards j in the set J_i the person holds. D_ijt = 1 if card j is 30+ days past due in month t. F_ijt = 1 if card j is the FIRST of i's cards to reach 30 DPD in the distress spell that starts in t.

(1) HIERARCHY, H. For the same person in the same month, holding both cards A and B, with at least one of them going late: H_i(A,B) = P(F_iA = 1 | i, t, holds A and B, some card goes late) - P(F_iB = 1 | same). Equivalently, a borrower's ranking pi_i over accounts, where card A ranks above card B if the borrower lets B slip first. Population version H(A,B) = E_i[H_i(A,B)] over multi-card distressed borrowers. Two sub-versions matter: H^raw does NOT hold the cards' terms fixed (this is what TransUnion product-level studies report: which product goes late first, terms and all); H^brand = H^raw conditional on each card's own contractual state (line, balance, APR, utilization, age) = the part of the ranking attributable to the label itself. "Priority / brand halo" in the user's sense is H^brand.

(2) BRAND EFFECT ON REPAYMENT, B. A card-level potential outcome: Y_ijt(b) = delinquency outcome on card j if the card carried label b, with the person, the month, and the card's own terms held fixed. B = E[Y_ijt(Amex) - Y_ijt(Synchrony)] over holders. B is a level effect on ONE card, not a within-person contrast; it bundles the borrower's ranking response (H^brand) with issuer-side effects (servicing, hardship programs, due-date design, 30-day reporting timing, re-aging).

(3) ISSUER EFFECT AT SAME FICO, Delta(f) (pool level; abs-risk track A). Delta(f) = E[Y | issuer = Amex, FICO = f] - E[Y | issuer = Synchrony, FICO = f], a descriptive contrast between two populations. Delta = Delta_selection (unobserved type theta at fixed FICO) + Delta_terms (lines, APR, rewards) + B (brand effect, which contains H^brand) + Delta_liquidity (differences in the holders' TOTAL available credit, including the free-riding channel) + issuer policy differences. The entry x conversion split in track A partitions Y, not these components. Only (1) is a within-person ranking; (2) and (3) are not hierarchy at all.
formal.model:
Notation. Person i, month t, cards j in J_i. Observed score f_i; unobserved creditworthiness theta_i. P_ij = 1 if card j carries the premium label (Amex); A_i = max_j P_ij = 1 if the person holds any premium badge.

Selection: P(A_i = 1 | theta_i, f_i) is increasing in theta_i at fixed f_i. (This is the "issuer sees more than FICO" story.)

Lines with free-riding and endogeneity, for every card j:
  L_ijt = l_j( f_i, s_j(theta_i), A_i, L_{i,-j,t-1} ) + u_ijt
  with gamma_j = dL_ijt/dA_i >= 0 for j not equal to the premium card (other lenders read the badge on the file, directly or through score attributes, and lend more), and rho_j = dL_ijt/dL_{i,-j,t-1} (each issuer's line responds to the other issuers' lines, e.g. through total revolving credit and utilization in the score). s_j(theta) is what issuer j privately sees of theta.

Liquidity: Q_it = sum_j (L_ijt - B_ijt) + M_it, total available credit plus cash. Free-riding raises Q_it by sum_{j != premium} gamma_j when A_i = 1.

Borrowing response: dB_ijt/dL_ijt = MPB(f_i); Agarwal et al. 2018 estimate MPB = 59% for FICO < 660 and about 0 for FICO > 740 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w21567). So the net liquidity gain from a line increase is (1 - MPB) per dollar, and the debt burden rises by MPB per dollar.

Person-month shock: e_it (income or expense shock). Distress: S_it = 1{ e_it - kappa(f_i) * Q_it - theta_i > 0 }. kappa > 0 for prime (more available credit lowers the chance any card goes late); for subprime the burden from the extra borrowing can dominate, so d P(S_it = 1) / d L can be positive. Agarwal et al.: a $1,000 limit increase raises 90+ DPD within 4 years by 1.16 pp on a base of 14.5% for FICO < 660, less than two-thirds of that for intermediate FICO, and close to zero for the highest FICO group (https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf, Section VII.B).

Card ranking in distress: protection value V_ijt = alpha_j(label) + beta_1 * (L_ijt - B_ijt) + beta_2 * (B_ijt / sum_k B_ikt) + eta_ijt. alpha_j is the brand / priority term (H^brand). beta_1 captures "available credit shifts the pecking order" (Andersson et al. 2013, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jmcb.12001); beta_2 captures the balance-share rule (Gathergood et al. 2019). The card with the lowest V goes late first: F_ijt = S_it * 1{ V_ijt = min_k V_ikt }.

Reduced form for one card: D_ijt = 1{ e_it - kappa Q_it - theta_i - alpha_j - beta x_ijt - eta_ijt > 0 }, with x_ijt the card's own terms.

The third channel is the path A_i -> L_{i,-j,t} (gamma) -> Q_it (kappa) -> D_ijt for EVERY card j, including the premium card itself. It is a person-month quantity. It also has a card-level footprint: gamma changes WHICH card has room, so it enters V_ijt through beta_1 and beta_2 on the other cards.

estimators.name: (a) Pool-level trust comparison at constant FICO mix (abs-risk track A)
estimators.description: Compare each master trust's monthly 30+ entry rate and 90+ to write-off conversion, reweighting or conditioning on FICO bands. abs-risk finds Amex entry 0.74% vs Synchrony 2.54% (ratio 0.29), conversion 44.8% vs 32.4% (ratio 1.38), and reads 'entry-side gap' as selection (C:/Users/samwe/code/abs-risk/docs/conclusions.html).
estimators.why: Proven by logic from the DGP: the third channel lowers P(S_it = 1) for premium-badge holders through kappa * Q_it, which reduces ENTRY on every card the person holds and leaves CONVERSION untouched. That is the identical signature the page assigns to selection. So track A's 'entry accounts for 124% of the gap' = selection + badge-induced liquidity + terms + any issuer policy that moves entry. The decomposition cannot tell these apart because it never observes a person. Direction: for the prime holders who dominate Amex's trust, kappa * (1 - MPB) is close to zero per Agarwal et al., so the channel adds little to Amex's low entry; for the subprime holders in Synchrony's or Capital One's trusts, a premium badge is rare, and where it exists the limit increases it triggers RAISE delinquency (+1.16 pp 90+ DPD per $1,000 for FICO < 660). Net, the channel plausibly widens the measured gap in the same direction as selection, but its size is unmeasured.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Even with the third channel removed: theta selection vs brand effect B vs terms vs issuer charge-off and re-aging policy (the page concedes the 1.38 conversion ratio could be Amex charging off faster). Also FICO scales differ across issuers and trust pools are the seasoned, securitised slice of the book, not the book.

estimators.name: (b) Cross-section: people with vs without an Amex, delinquency on their OTHER cards
estimators.description: Regress D_ijt on non-Amex cards on A_i with FICO controls, bureau panel.
estimators.why: Proven by logic: A_i is chosen on theta (selection), and the coefficient on A_i is the sum of (i) selection on theta, (ii) the third channel gamma * kappa on the other cards, and (iii) the priority substitution: if the person protects the Amex, the other cards slip FIRST, which raises other-card delinquency. (ii) and (iii) have opposite signs for prime borrowers, so even the sign of the total is uninformative about either. The strongest published analogue, Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania (JFE 2021, https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v142y2021i2p719-736.html), needed an instrument (loan-officer leniency) precisely because the cross-section is uninterpretable.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Everything: selection on theta, income, the number and terms of other cards, and the priority substitution.

estimators.name: (c) Within-person, across-card comparison without time effects (person fixed effect only)
estimators.description: Regress D_ijt on an issuer dummy with person fixed effects, pooling all months.
estimators.why: Proven by logic: the person FE removes theta_i and the time-average of Q_it, but Q_it varies month to month and cards are held over different windows. Badge acquisition is timed with good liquidity (people get an Amex when doing well), and the other lenders' line increases arrive AFTER the badge, so months in which the Amex is held have higher Q_it than months in which it is not. The issuer dummy then absorbs the within-person change in liquidity around the badge, which is the third channel itself. Free-riding also changes the other cards' lines, so the across-card term-differences are badge-induced.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Card-level terms (line, balance share, APR), card age, issuer policy, and any person-month shock not common to all card-months.

estimators.name: (d) Within-person, within-month (borrower x month fixed effects) comparison of cards, with an issuer dummy (Antoniou-Lyman-Pagel-Stewart design)
estimators.description: Sample: borrowers with several cards that go delinquent in the same billing cycle; borrower-by-year-month fixed effects; card-level regressor = issuer label (Antoniou et al. use charged-off vs cured cards, UK FCA data, 1.6M borrowers, 5 issuers, 2013-2014; https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5121519 and https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2026/program/paper/GSdFHD5h). For hierarchy, replace the outcome with F_ijt (which card slips first) or with within-spell repayment on card j.
estimators.why: Proven by logic from the DGP: Q_it, e_it, theta_i, and every other person-month quantity, including the ENTIRE liquidity path A_i -> other lines -> Q_it, are constant across the person's cards inside one month and are absorbed by the borrower x month fixed effect. Whatever the badge did to the person's total liquidity cannot move a contrast between two cards held by the same person in the same month. This is the whole point: hierarchy is a within-person ranking, and the third channel is a person-level shift. The claim that free-riding 'harms the ability to come up with a payment hierarchy estimator' is false for this design.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: The issuer dummy still equals alpha_j + beta * E[x_ijt - x_ikt | labels, i, t]: the difference in card TERMS between the Amex and the other card, which is (i) partly caused by the label (Amex gives larger lines; charge cards have no revolving room) and (ii) partly caused by free-riding, because the other lenders' response to the badge changes which card has room and which carries the balance share. Andersson et al. 2013 and Gathergood et al. 2019 show those two things drive the ordering. So the dummy in (d) is H^raw for the label, not H^brand. Also confounded: issuer-side timing (30-day reporting conventions, due-date alignment, autopay defaults, hardship programs), and the sample is conditioned on distress (LATE for multi-card distressed borrowers, which is the population hierarchy is about, so acceptable).

estimators.name: (e) Design (d) plus card line and balance controls
estimators.description: Same as (d) with L_ijt, B_ijt, utilization, APR, card age as card-level controls.
estimators.why: This is the right specification for H^brand: conditioning on the card's own terms removes the mediated path (label -> terms -> ranking) and leaves alpha_j. Free-riding enters only through terms, and terms are now held fixed. But lines and balances are POST-treatment and endogenous to the distress: Antoniou et al. document that after a default on one card, the borrower's other cards' limits fall by an average of GBP 700 and their bureau charge-off score rises about 10% (Figure 5 in the Nov 2025 draft). Contemporaneous lines therefore carry the issuers' reaction to the spell. Use lines and balances measured BEFORE the spell (e.g. 3 to 6 months before the first 30 DPD), or the issuer's line-assignment discontinuities as instruments (Agarwal et al. style).
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Issuer-side servicing and reporting practices (the same 30-day event is created by the issuer's grace and reporting rules), unobserved card-level attributes the borrower values (rewards, acceptance, autopay), and the fact that a charge card's 'line' is undefined.

estimators.name: (f) Regression discontinuity at the premium issuer's approval cutoff; outcome = repayment on OTHER lenders' accounts
estimators.description: Applicants to Amex just above vs below the score cutoff; outcomes on their pre-existing non-Amex tradelines over the next 12-24 months; mediators = other lenders' lines.
estimators.why: Not biased: the RD identifies the total causal effect of holding the badge on other-card outcomes, and the third channel is part of the estimand, not a confounder. It is the design that MEASURES the channel, provided one records the mediator (other lenders' lines after approval) and splits by FICO band. It does NOT identify H (which card slips first) unless combined with (d) on the approved applicants' cards. Two warnings from Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania (2016 draft, https://www.stern.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/assets/documents/NYU-Liberman-Borrower%20reputation_0.pdf): the brief's summary of that paper is slightly wrong. Their score and credit-rationing effects come from the loan-officer-leniency IV for the AVERAGE applicant (score -4.7% in the quarter of application, about -10% at four quarters, with no worsening of contemporaneous repayment); at the approval CUTOFF the RD gives a precise ZERO on scores, on default, and on rationing, because the marginal applicant was already tagged high-risk. The lesson for Amex: the label's signal value is heterogeneous and can be smallest exactly at the cutoff, so a cutoff RD may return a null even if free-riding is large away from it. Second, abs-risk's own attempt at lender cutoffs found half failed density tests and the rest were underpowered.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Net of two opposite-signed effects on other cards: third channel (lowers other-card delinquency for prime) and priority substitution (raises it, since the Amex is protected). Separating them needs the mediator (lines) and timing: line effects arrive within months for everyone; substitution shows only in distress spells.

estimators.name: (g) Portfolio-transfer event study (same accounts, new issuer brand: e.g. Costco Amex -> Citi 2016, Walmart Synchrony -> Capital One 2019)
estimators.description: Same borrowers, same accounts, label changes on a known date; compare the transferred card's delinquency before and after, relative to the borrower's other cards or matched accounts.
estimators.why: It is the cleanest design for B (person and initial terms held fixed), but the third channel re-enters: the tradeline's furnisher name changes on the file, so other lenders may re-read it (a Synchrony line becomes a Capital One line, or a Citi line stops being an Amex line) and adjust their lines, which moves Q_it for these borrowers after the event. Plausible but unmeasured. Adding borrower x month fixed effects over the borrower's other cards removes that, at the cost of restricting to multi-card borrowers.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: The acquirer re-underwrites, changes lines, APRs, rewards, collections intensity, and charge-off timing, usually within a year; the event therefore mixes borrower priority with issuer policy. Any cardholder churn triggered by the transfer (people who close the card or move spending) is selection on the outcome. Whether transfers are announced in advance also matters (anticipation).

formal.claim_verdict:
Partly true, and the true part does not land where the user put it.

TRUE (proven by logic, with published support for the mechanism): (1) Other lenders read lender identity on the file. Evidence for a NEGATIVE label: FICO reason code 06 'too many consumer finance company accounts' (https://www.trudiligence.com/docs/ficoscorefactors.pdf); Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania (JFE 2021) find a UK high-cost loan cuts the average applicant's score by 4.7% in the quarter of take-up with no contemporaneous change in repayment, and reduces later bank credit; Antoniou et al. (2025) find a default on one card lowers the borrower's OTHER cards' limits by about GBP 700. Evidence for a POSITIVE premium badge raising other lenders' lines: none located; plausible but unmeasured. (2) That channel is a person-level liquidity shift, and it is observationally identical to selection in every design that does not observe a person: the abs-risk pool-level entry x conversion split (a), the cross-section (b), and the person-FE-without-time design (c). So 'selection, not close' should read 'entry-side, not close; the entry side contains selection, terms, and any badge-induced liquidity, which the filings cannot separate.' (3) Each card's line is endogenous to every other lender's line (via utilization and total-credit attributes) and to the borrower's distress (limits fall after a default), so a contemporaneous line is an outcome, not a control.

FALSE: (1) 'Free riding harms the ability to come up with a payment hierarchy estimator.' Hierarchy is a within-person, within-month ranking. The third channel is common to all of the person's cards in a month and is absorbed by the borrower x month fixed effect (design d). No person-level quantity, including badge-induced liquidity, can bias a contrast between two cards the same person holds in the same month. What survives in (d) is a card-level residue (the badge changes which card has room and which carries the balance share), which is observable and handled by pre-spell line and balance controls (design e). The hierarchy estimator exists and is not harmed; what free-riding contaminates is the pool-level 'issuer effect at same FICO' and the cross-sectional 'brand effect', which are different estimands the user has been conflating with hierarchy. (2) The implied magnitude for the Amex-vs-Synchrony gap is probably small on the Amex side: Agarwal et al. 2018 find a $1,000 limit increase has close to zero effect on delinquency for FICO > 740 (and MPB about 0), so extra lines elsewhere barely move a prime holder's entry rate; the channel's repayment leg is strongest for FICO < 660, where premium badges are rare. This is (b)-level evidence for the leg and (c)-level for the badge's line response, so the size stays unknown, but the sign is not in dispute: it works in the same direction as selection.

Also a correction to the brief: Liberman et al.'s score and rationing effects are for the average applicant via loan-officer-leniency IV, NOT at the approval cutoff; at the cutoff the RD is a precise zero for scores, default, and rationing.
formal.third_channel_statement: The third channel is the path: premium label on person i's file (A_i = 1) -> other lenders j read it, directly or through score attributes, and raise their lines by gamma_j (free-riding on the first lender's screening) -> the person's total available credit Q_it rises by sum_j gamma_j * (1 - MPB(f_i)) net of the borrowing it induces -> the probability that ANY card goes late in a bad month, P(S_it = 1), falls by kappa(f_i) times that amount for prime borrowers, and can rise for subprime borrowers because the induced borrowing (MPB = 59% below FICO 660) raises the debt burden (Agarwal et al. 2018: +1.16 pp 90+ DPD per $1,000 for FICO < 660, about zero for FICO > 740). It enters the delinquency equation of EVERY card the person holds, including the premium card itself, as the person-month term kappa * Q_it. Where it enters each estimator: it sits inside the ENTRY rate in pool comparisons (a), inside the coefficient on A_i in cross-sections (b), inside the issuer dummy in person-FE-only panels (c), and inside the estimand (not the error) in an approval-cutoff RD on other cards (f). It is absorbed entirely by borrower x month fixed effects (d), leaving only a card-level residue: the badge changes which of the person's cards has spare room and which carries the balance share, and those two things shift the ordering (Andersson et al. 2013; Gathergood et al. 2019). That residue is removed by conditioning on pre-spell lines and balances (e). The published evidence for the first leg (label -> other lenders' lines) is for NEGATIVE labels (payday tradeline, a prior default); for a positive premium badge it is plausible but unmeasured.
formal.line_endogeneity_statement: Each card's line is a function of the other lenders' lines and of the person's current distress, so it is an outcome, not a control. Formally L_ijt = l_j(f_i, s_j(theta_i), A_i, L_{i,-j,t-1}) + u_ijt with rho_j = dL_ijt / dL_{i,-j,t-1} not zero: issuers see total revolving credit and utilization across all cards in the score and in bureau attributes, and they see the labels of the other furnishers. Two consequences. (1) Line differences across a person's cards are partly caused by the labels on the other cards, so a within-person 'issuer effect' that does not condition on lines includes a badge-induced terms difference (H^raw, not H^brand). (2) Contemporaneous lines respond to the spell itself: Antoniou et al. (2025) show other cards' limits fall by about GBP 700 after a default on one card and the bureau charge-off score rises about 10%, so adding same-month lines as controls is conditioning on a post-treatment variable. Remedies: use lines measured before the distress spell, or use the issuer's own line-assignment discontinuities (Agarwal et al. 2018 use 743 such cutoffs) as instruments for the line. Note this endogeneity is standard and would exist without any free-riding on labels; the label channel is one of several reasons rho_j is non-zero.
formal.what_would_prove_magnitude:
Data: a monthly consumer-level bureau or consortium panel with issuer identity on each tradeline, per-tradeline line, balance, and 30/60/90 DPD status, and FICO (FRBNY/Equifax CCP, a TransUnion or Argus 'wallet view' panel, or the UK FCA CCPS data Gathergood et al. and Antoniou et al. use). The abs-risk 10-D data cannot do this; nothing observing one person with two accounts is public.

Design, in three parts, each producing a number:
(1) The first leg, gamma: other lenders' line response to a premium badge. Event study of the borrower's PRE-EXISTING non-Amex lines in the 12 months after an Amex account opens, against matched borrowers (same FICO, utilization, income proxy, month) who did not open one, with pre-trends checked. Better: an approval-cutoff RD or an issuer's lottery/leniency variation at the premium issuer, with other lenders' lines as the outcome, estimated separately by FICO band (Liberman et al. show the signal effect is heterogeneous and can be zero at the cutoff). Report gamma in dollars of other-lender line per badge, by FICO band.
(2) The second leg, dD/dQ: take from Agarwal et al. 2018 by FICO band (close to zero above 740; +1.16 pp 90+ DPD per $1,000 below 660), or re-estimate on the same panel using line-assignment discontinuities.
(3) The product gamma * (1 - MPB) * dD/dQ by FICO band is the third-channel contribution to each issuer's entry rate; reweight to each trust's FICO mix and compare with the observed entry gap (Amex 0.74% vs Synchrony 2.54% per month). If gamma for prime holders is a few thousand dollars and dD/dQ is about zero above 740, the channel explains close to none of Amex's low entry, and the residual is selection plus terms plus issuer policy.

For hierarchy itself: run design (d)/(e) on the same panel with the outcome F_ijt (which card slips first in a synchronous distress spell), an issuer-label regressor, and pre-spell lines and balance shares as controls. The gap between the label coefficient with and without the pre-spell term controls is the badge-induced terms residue of the third channel; the coefficient with the controls is H^brand. A portfolio transfer (same accounts, new label) with borrower x month fixed effects over the borrower's other cards gives an independent check on B.
key_assumptions: Hierarchy is defined as a within-person, within-month ranking of accounts; any estimand that compares different people is not hierarchy.

The free-riding channel acts on the person's total liquidity Q_it, which is common to all cards the person holds in month t (so it is absorbed by borrower x month fixed effects). Its only card-level footprint is through card terms (room and balance share).

Delinquency on each card falls with total available credit for prime borrowers and can rise with limit increases for subprime borrowers; the sign and size by FICO band are taken from Agarwal et al. 2018 (MPB 59% below 660, about zero above 740; +1.16 pp 90+ DPD per $1,000 below 660, close to zero at the top), a single-issuer US sample 2008-2013.

Other lenders can and do read furnisher identity on the file. Published evidence is for negative labels (FICO reason code 06; payday tradeline in Liberman et al.; a prior default in Antoniou et al.). The positive premium-badge response gamma is assumed non-negative and is unmeasured.

Card lines are post-treatment: they respond to other lenders' lines and to the borrower's distress (limits fall about GBP 700 after a default on another card per Antoniou et al.). Valid line controls are pre-spell lines or instrumented lines.

Issuer-side policies (30-day reporting conventions, grace periods, hardship programs, charge-off timing, re-aging) are constant within issuer and are NOT separately identified from borrower ranking in any of the designs without issuer-level policy data.
Selection: at fixed FICO, the probability of holding a premium badge increases in unobserved creditworthiness theta; this is what pool-level and cross-sectional designs cannot remove.
The borrower x month design conditions on distress (at least one card late in the month), so its estimand is for multi-card distressed borrowers; this is the population hierarchy is about.

The abs-risk track A numbers (Amex entry ratio 0.29, conversion ratio 1.38 vs Synchrony; 554 trust-months, 2018-2026) are taken as reported at C:/Users/samwe/code/abs-risk/docs/conclusions.html and not re-derived.

Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania's score effect (-4.7% same quarter, about -10% at four quarters) is for the average applicant via loan-officer-leniency IV; the approval-cutoff RD gives a precise zero. Signal effects of a label are therefore heterogeneous in the prior credit score.

refutation.strongest_objection: The formalization's central "proven by logic" claims rest on a sign assumption (kappa > 0: more available credit lowers the chance any card goes late) that the only causal evidence it cites points against. Agarwal-Chomsisengphet-Mahoney-Stroebel Table VI (https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf) shows a $1,000 limit increase RAISES 90+ DPD within 4 years by 1.16 pp (base 14.5%) for FICO <= 660, by under two-thirds of that for intermediate FICO, and is "close to zero" for the top group; no FICO group shows a decline, and the outcome is delinquency on the treated account itself, not on the person's other cards. So the third channel as written (badge -> more lines elsewhere -> lower entry on every card) has zero published support in that direction for anyone; the supported net effect of extra lines on entry is zero to positive. That flips the author's directional conclusions: the channel cannot be said to "work in the same direction as selection" or to "widen the measured gap"; if it operates at all it weakly RAISES badge holders' entry, making the observed 0.29 Amex/Synchrony entry ratio a conservative reading of selection-plus-terms, not an inflated one. And the companion claim that the channel "leaves CONVERSION untouched" and therefore carries "the identical signature to selection" is not derived from the DGP (which has no 30->90->write-off transition structure at all); if liquidity also affects cure from 90+, the channel would LOWER conversion for badge holders, the opposite of Amex's observed 1.38x. So "biased by free-riding, proven by logic" for estimator (a) collapses to "unidentified, sign unknown, probably small for prime" -- which the prior review had already said.
errors_found: SIGN / EVIDENCE ERROR (model, estimator a, claim_verdict, third_channel_statement): kappa > 0 for prime is asserted and then used to conclude the channel lowers Amex entry and 'works in the same direction as selection'. ACMS Table VI (https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf) finds limit increases raise own-account delinquency (+1.21 pp 60+ DPD on base 16.5%, +1.16 pp 90+ DPD on base 14.5%, FICO <= 660, 4-year horizon), smaller positive for intermediate, ~0 for the top group; never negative. The net sign of the channel on entry is therefore zero-to-positive per the only cited causal estimate, so the directional sentences are unsupported. The 'same direction as selection' claim also double-counts: a subprime person holding a rare Amex badge who gets extra lines elsewhere and goes late also goes late on the Amex card, which sits in Amex's trust, so the composition argument does not sign the pool gap either.

UNDERIVED ASSERTION (estimator a): 'lowers ENTRY on every card and leaves CONVERSION untouched ... identical signature to selection'. The stated DGP is a one-period threshold D_ijt with no transition structure; nothing in it implies liquidity affects 30-DPD entry but not cure from 90+. If liquidity aids cure (balance transfers, paying from other lines), the channel lowers conversion for badge holders, opposite to Amex's 1.38x conversion ratio. 'Proven by logic' is overstated; it is an extra assumption.

OUTCOME MISMATCH (model, what_would_prove_magnitude): ACMS measure delinquency on the treated account ('probability of an account being more than 90 days past due', Table VI header) after that account's own limit rises. The formalization uses this as dD/dQ for delinquency on OTHER cards (including the Amex card in Amex's trust) after OTHER lenders raise lines. ACMS say nothing about spillover to other accounts; that leg is unmeasured, not 'taken from Agarwal et al.'

PROOF BY CONSTRUCTION (estimator d, key_assumptions 2): 'No person-level quantity ... can bias a contrast between two cards the same person holds in the same month' is true only because the DGP puts Q_it additively and identically into every card's index V_ijt. Any interaction of liquidity with the label's protection value (e.g. borrowers juggle to protect the Amex only when they have room elsewhere) is not absorbed by borrower x month FE. Two further gaps: (i) design (d) conditions on S_it = 1, and the third channel changes P(S_it = 1) per person, so it changes WHICH badge holders and which shock sizes e_it enter the estimation sample; with heterogeneous alpha the FE estimate is a different average with vs without free-riding (not bias for the conditional estimand as defined, but the blanket sentence is false as a general statement); (ii) in any nonlinear link the person-month index level scales the marginal effect of the card dummy. The absorption result should be stated as 'holds under additive separability and homogeneous label effects'.

SIGNABLE BUT UNSIGNED RESIDUE (estimator d, third_channel_statement): the author calls the card-level footprint of free-riding a residue of unknown direction. Under the author's own DGP it is signed: gamma_j > 0 raises L on the NON-Amex cards; with beta_1 > 0 (borrowers protect cards that still have room, the Andersson et al. reading), those cards' protection value V rises, so the Amex slips first more often. Free-riding therefore biases the Amex 'priority' coefficient in (d) DOWNWARD, toward 'Amex not protected'. This is the one concrete sense in which the user's claim is right: an H^raw hierarchy estimate understates Amex brand halo by an amount proportional to gamma * beta_1, and that amount is unmeasured. Note also that Andersson et al. 2013 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/jmoncb/v45y2013i2-3p251-275.html) study the MORTGAGE-vs-card pecking order ('illiquidity in the form of available credit'), not card-vs-card; beta_1 for cards is extrapolated.

ESTIMAND SLIPPAGE (estimator e, claim_verdict FALSE(1)): the author says the hierarchy estimator 'is not harmed' because (e) recovers H^brand by conditioning on pre-spell lines and balances. But the pre-spell lines on the other cards are outcomes of the badge (gamma), so conditioning on them removes the free-riding path BY DEFINITION of H^brand (a mediator is held fixed), not by identification. Worse, the author's own line_endogeneity_statement says a line 'is an outcome, not a control' because L_ijt contains s_j(theta_i) and u_ijt; pre-spell timing fixes the post-distress reaction (the GBP 700 fall) but not the within-person correlation between u_ijt and eta_ijt (an issuer that privately sees the borrower's spending gives a bigger line and is also the card the borrower values). So (e) is a controlled regression with an endogenous mediator, and 'biased_by_free_riding: false' for (e) is not established; H^brand needs an exogenous line shifter (the ACMS-style cutoff instrument the author mentions but does not build into the design).

SAMPLE MISMATCH (estimator d description): Antoniou et al. (Nov 20 2025 draft, https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2026/program/paper/GSdFHD5h) identify from borrowers 'who go delinquent on multiple credit cards simultaneously (in the same billing cycle)' with some but not all later charged off, using borrower-by-year-month FE. That sample is exactly where F_ijt (which card slips FIRST) is a tie. 'Replace the outcome with F_ijt' requires a different sample (>= 1 card late, >= 1 not) in which F is a one-of-J indicator per person-month, i.e. a conditional-logit / discrete-choice problem over the person's card set, identified only from persons holding both labels, not a linear FE regression with an issuer dummy. The design is workable but is not the Antoniou design.

MIS-STATEMENT OF SOURCE (estimator e, line_endogeneity_statement): the '+10%' in Antoniou et al. Figure 5 is the issuer's risk-band 'Charged-off rate' ('the credit card provider determined probability that a borrower in that particular risk band will default'), not a bureau charge-off score. The GBP 700 limit fall and ~1 pp APR fall are correctly quoted.

OVER-TRANSFER OF LIBERMAN HETEROGENEITY (estimator f): LPP's cutoff zero occurs at an eligibility score of 400 where applicants are 'pooled with riskier individuals' so the signal cannot fall further (https://www.stern.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/assets/documents/NYU-Liberman-Borrower%20reputation_0.pdf). Amex's cutoff sits in prime territory, and for a POSITIVE badge the marginal applicant is plausibly where the first lender's private information matters most. 'Signal value can be smallest exactly at the cutoff' does not transfer; direction at an Amex cutoff is unknown. Also the formalization cites the 2016 draft ('leads to more default' for the average applicant) while the published JFE 2021 abstract (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v142y2021i2p719-736.html) says take-up 'does not affect future debt repayment'; cite the published version.

'LENDER IDENTITY' OVERSTATED (claim_verdict TRUE(1), key_assumptions 4): FICO reason code 06 penalizes an account TYPE (consumer finance company, an industry classification in the bureau file), and LPP's payday tradeline is likewise an industry type. Neither shows a scoring model or prescreen reading a specific furnisher name such as 'American Express'. Evidence that lenders read furnisher IDENTITY: none located; the verdict sentence 'Other lenders read lender identity on the file' should say 'lender type'.

EMPIRICAL CLAIM DRESSED AS LOGIC (estimator c): 'Badge acquisition is timed with good liquidity' and 'other lenders' line increases arrive AFTER the badge' are unmeasured assertions used to sign the person-FE bias. Plausible, category (c), not 'proven by logic'.

MAGNITUDE INPUTS UNVERIFIED: ACMS bureau data at the average quasi-experiment show holders with 11 cards, $33,533 total limits, $9,551 total balances (PDF Section III). Against that base, a badge-induced line response of 'a few thousand dollars' (the author's illustrative gamma) is a small share of Q_it even before multiplying by a ~0 dD/dQ for prime; the author should state this rather than leave gamma unanchored.
refutation.what_survives: (1) The three-estimand taxonomy (H within-person ranking; B card-level brand effect; Delta pool-level issuer effect at same FICO) is correct and useful, and the point that abs-risk track A measures Delta, not H, stands. (2) Proven by logic: the abs-risk entry x conversion split (0.74% vs 2.54% entry, 44.8% vs 32.4% conversion, ratios 0.29 and 1.38, entry share 124%, C:/Users/samwe/code/abs-risk/docs/conclusions.html) cannot separate selection on theta from ANY person-level liquidity difference, from terms, or from issuer policy, because it never observes a person; 'selection, not close' should read 'entry-side, not close'. This was already known and the formalization restates it correctly. (3) Supported by published numbers: lender type is read on the file for NEGATIVE labels (LPP: -4.7% score in the application quarter, -10% at four quarters via leniency IV, precise zero at the score-400 cutoff; Antoniou et al.: other cards' limits -GBP 700 and issuer risk-band charge-off rate +~10% after a default on one card). (4) Line endogeneity is real and standard: contemporaneous lines respond to other lenders' lines and to distress, so same-month lines are post-treatment controls; pre-spell lines fix the distress reaction but not the private-information correlation. (5) A within-person, within-month design does exist and does absorb any ADDITIVE person-level liquidity term; an unbiased estimator of H^raw (the label's total within-person effect on which card slips first, free-riding residue included) is available from a discrete-choice version of design (d). (6) ACMS numbers as quoted (MPB 59% below 660, ~0 above 740, 743 cutoffs, +1.16 pp 90+ DPD per $1,000 on base 14.5%) are accurate. (7) The corrected reading of LPP (IV for the average applicant, RD zero at the cutoff) is accurate.
refutation.corrected_verdict: The user's claim ('free riding harms the ability to come up with a payment hierarchy estimator') is mostly wrong as stated, but the formalization's rebuttal is overstated in four places and should be replaced by the following. (A) Pool-level and cross-sectional designs (abs-risk track A, any A_i regression) cannot separate selection from a badge-induced liquidity channel; that is true but was already known, and it is NOT proven that the channel mimics selection's entry-not-conversion signature: the DGP has no transition structure, and the only causal evidence on lines and delinquency (ACMS Table VI) says extra lines weakly RAISE own-account delinquency for FICO <= 660 and do ~nothing above 740, never lower it. So the channel's contribution to Amex's low entry is 'unknown, probably near zero for prime holders, and if nonzero it works AGAINST the observed gap'; the 0.29 entry ratio is a conservative reading of selection-plus-terms, not an inflated one. Drop 'same direction as selection'. (B) For hierarchy proper: borrower x month fixed effects absorb the person-level liquidity term under additive separability and homogeneous label effects (an assumption, not a theorem), and an estimator of H^raw exists (conditional-logit over the person's card set on months with >= 1 late and >= 1 current card; the Antoniou synchronous-delinquency sample is the wrong sample because F is a tie there). What free-riding does do, under the author's own DGP with beta_1 > 0, is raise the non-Amex cards' room and therefore bias the Amex priority coefficient in H^raw DOWNWARD; separating H^brand from that requires an exogenous shifter of other-card lines (issuer line-assignment cutoffs), because pre-spell lines remain endogenous within person through issuers' private information. So the honest sentence is: 'free-riding does not prevent a hierarchy estimator; it makes the measured Amex priority a lower bound on the brand halo by an unmeasured amount, and closing the gap needs instrumented lines, not controls'. (C) Evidence status: label reading on the file is documented for lender TYPE and negative labels only (FICO code 06, LPP payday tradeline, Antoniou post-default limit cuts); a positive premium-badge line response gamma is plausible but unmeasured, and the LPP 'zero at the cutoff' does not transfer to an Amex cutoff in prime territory. (D) The line-endogeneity point survives intact and is the part of the user's intuition worth keeping: each card's line is an outcome of every other lender's read of the file and of the borrower's distress, so line differences across a person's cards are never valid controls without an instrument. Net: refuted as 'harms the estimator'; survives as 'signs a downward bias on measured Amex priority in any within-person design that does not instrument other-card lines, and is unidentified from selection in every pool-level design'.

formal.estimand:
Three different targets, which the current write-up runs together.

(1) HIERARCHY (person-level, relative). For person i, in month t, holding cards A and B and current on both at the start of t, under a cash shortfall:
  H_i,t(A,B) = P(A is the FIRST card of i to reach 30+ DPD in t | i stressed, i's total liquidity L_it, both current at t-1) minus the same for B.
Population version: average of H over multi-card holders who are in stress. Equivalent ranking form: r_i(A) < r_i(B) means i lets B slip before A. This is a within-person, within-month comparison. It is defined CONDITIONAL on the person's total liquidity L_it and the shock s_it, because those are the same for both cards. It says nothing about how many people get into stress.

(2) BRAND EFFECT ON REPAYMENT (card-level, causal, level). For a fixed account j held by person i with line L_j, balance B_ijt, APR, and all of i's other accounts held fixed:
  BE_j = E[ D_ijt | plastic says Amex ] - E[ D_ijt | plastic says Synchrony ], D = 1[30+ DPD].
This is "same account, same person, same everything, different label". It includes label, perceived status, and issuer servicing behaviour. It is what a portfolio-transfer event study aims at.

(3) ISSUER EFFECT AT SAME FICO (pool-level, descriptive). 
  IE(f) = E[ D | issuer = Amex, FICO = f ] - E[ D | issuer = Synchrony, FICO = f ], then averaged over f.
This is a difference in means between DIFFERENT PEOPLE. It equals: selection on things FICO does not see + line/balance/utilization composition + hierarchy (1) + brand (2) + the third channel below. It is not a causal effect of anything. The abs-risk trust comparison (Amex 30+ share = 0.29x Synchrony; 90+ to write-off conversion = 1.38x; source: C:/Users/samwe/code/abs-risk/docs/conclusions.html) is a version of (3) with no FICO conditioning at all, since 10-D filings do not carry FICO.
formal.model:
Indices: person i, month t, card j in J_i, issuer b(j). Premium badge G_i = 1 if i holds an Amex-type card.

Person primitives:
  theta_i = creditworthiness. FICO sees f_i; issuer b additionally sees a private signal eta_ib (its own transaction, relationship, or application data).
  s_it = person-month liquidity shock (job loss, medical bill). Same for every card.

Badge selection (the SELECTION story):
  G_i = 1[ a0 + a1*f_i + a2*eta_i,Amex + u_i > c ].   (a2 > 0 is what "selection on information beyond FICO" means.)

Lines with FREE-RIDING and LINE ENDOGENEITY (for every non-premium issuer b):
  L_j = lam0 + lam_f*f_i + lam_G*G_i + lam_L*sum_{k != j} L_k + lam_eta*eta_ib + e_j.
  lam_G = free-riding coefficient: the issuer's model or prescreen reads "has an Amex tradeline" as a positive signal. (Mirror image with lam_G < 0 is the measured payday case: Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304405X21003299; FICO reason code 06 "too many consumer finance company accounts", https://www.trudiligence.com/docs/ficoscorefactors.pdf.)
  lam_L = line endogeneity: each issuer conditions on bureau-visible total limits/utilization set by the others. In matrix form L = Lam*L + lam_G*G*1 + ... so L = (I - Lam)^{-1}(...): every card's line is a function of every issuer's reading of the file, including the badge.

Total liquidity (person-month):
  Liq_it = cash_it + sum_j (L_j - B_ijt).

Balances follow lines with a FICO-dependent marginal propensity to borrow (Agarwal-Chomsisengphet-Mahoney-Stroebel QJE 2018: MPB 0.59 per $1 of limit for FICO <= 660, ~0 for FICO > 740; https://www.nber.org/papers/w21567):
  B_ijt = m(f_i)*L_j + (balance-matching share of the person's total debt, Gathergood et al. AER 2019, https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faer.20180288) + v_ijt.

Delinquency on card j (latent index):
  y*_ijt = alpha_i + gamma_t + s_it - beta(f_i)*Liq_it + kappa(f_i)*B_ijt/L_j + pi_b(j) + rho*(B_ijt / sum_k B_ikt) + xi_b(j) + eps_ijt
  D_ijt = 1[y*_ijt > 0].
  beta(f) >= 0: liquidity lowers delinquency, larger for prime. kappa(f) > 0 and large for subprime: higher lines -> higher balances -> higher delinquency (ACMS: a $1,000 limit increase raises 4-year 90+ DPD by 1.16 pp on a 14.5% base for FICO <= 660, near zero for FICO > 740; $1 of limit adds 21.6 cents of charge-offs at <= 660 vs 3.7 cents at > 740; https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf, Section VII.B and Table VII). Net effect of a line increase on delinquency = -beta*dLiq + kappa*m*d(utilization): negative for prime, positive for subprime.
  pi_b = brand/priority term (the card the person protects). rho = balance-share term (which card carries the debt). xi_b = issuer servicing/collections effect (outreach, hardship programs, autopay).
  Hierarchy is the ordering of (pi_b(j) + rho*share_ijt + kappa*util_ijt + xi_b(j) + eps_ijt) across j within (i,t); everything indexed only by (i,t) -- alpha_i, gamma_t, s_it, beta*Liq_it -- drops out of that ordering.

THIRD CHANNEL path: G_i -> L_k for k != Amex (lam_G) -> Liq_it and B_ikt -> D_ijt for ALL j, sign depending on f_i. It enters the delinquency equation only through Liq_it (a person-month scalar) and through the card-level utilization of the cards whose lines moved.

estimators.name: (a) Pool-level trust comparison at constant FICO mix (abs-risk track A)
estimators.description: Compare monthly 30+ entry rate and 90+ to write-off conversion across master trusts, reweighting or assuming a fixed FICO mix. Target is estimand (3).
estimators.why: Proven by logic from the DGP: the pool difference between Amex holders and Synchrony holders averages over DIFFERENT PEOPLE, so every person-level term differs between the two pools, including beta(f)*Liq_it. If lam_G > 0, Amex holders have larger lines at other lenders than otherwise-identical non-holders, hence more liquidity, hence lower entry on every card including the Amex card. That liquidity was created by other lenders' reading of the badge, not by Amex's screening (selection) and not by the person protecting the card (priority). It lands in the 'entry' residual that the conclusions page attributes to selection. Direction for the mostly-prime Amex book: makes Amex look MORE selected than it is. For a subprime book the ACMS sign flips (more line -> more delinquency), so for Synchrony a negative store-card badge could either help or hurt its entry rate; sign unknown.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Even with lam_G = 0: (i) selection on eta vs priority pi_b are both in the entry gap, as the prior review noted; (ii) line/balance/utilization composition (Amex lines and charge-card pay-in-full products vs small store-card lines) is in the entry gap; (iii) the conversion ratio conditions on a post-treatment event (already 90+). Under priority, the people who let a PROTECTED card reach 90+ are the ones with nothing left, so priority predicts a HIGH conversion rate on the protected card, not a low one. The 1.38x is therefore consistent with priority as well as selection; the decomposition does not identify. (iv) No FICO in 10-D data, so 'constant FICO mix' is an assumption, not a control. (v) Issuer servicing xi_b (hardship programs, re-aging rules, charge-off timing policy) is fully in the conversion ratio.

estimators.name: (b) Cross-section of people with vs without an Amex, delinquency on their OTHER cards
estimators.description: Compare 30+ rates on non-Amex cards between Amex holders and non-holders at the same FICO. Often read as 'the Amex-selected person is a better payer everywhere'.
estimators.why: Proven by logic: the other cards' lines are an OUTCOME of G_i (lam_G term), so the comparison bundles (1) selection on eta (Amex holders are better on unobservables), (2) badge-induced liquidity on the other cards, (3) balance shifting to the new card. Nothing in the cross-section separates them; the cross-section is the cleanest illustration of the user's claim. Empirical support for the mechanism, with the opposite-signed badge: taking a UK payday loan cut the average applicant's score 4.7% in the application quarter and 10% four quarters later while default in the application quarter fell about 11% (not significant) and debt-collection searches fell 16% (2016 WP version, https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/100_Liberman_HighCostCreditAndBorrowerReputation....pdf; JFE 2021 abstract: lower score and less future bank credit with no change in repayment, and no effect among borrowers already tagged high-risk, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304405X21003299). No published number exists for a POSITIVE premium badge; magnitude unknown.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Selection on eta, reverse causation (people who already had large lines elsewhere are more likely to be approved by Amex), and the mechanical utilization channel (a new $10k line lowers total utilization and raises FICO regardless of who issued it).

estimators.name: (c) Within-person across-card comparison without time effects
estimators.description: Person fixed effects; compare delinquency on i's Amex card vs i's other cards across all months i holds them.
estimators.why: Partly, and the mechanism is timing: Liq_it varies over time, and it changes exactly when the badge is acquired (other lenders' lines respond to the new tradeline over the following months). Without month-by-person effects, card-months before and after the badge are pooled; the other cards' post-badge months are lower-delinquency for prime people, and the Amex card only exists in post-badge months. The issuer contrast therefore mixes card identity with a time-varying person-level liquidity path caused by the badge. Smaller than (a)/(b) because alpha_i is removed, but not zero.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Card-level line, balance share, utilization, product type (charge card vs revolving), card age, and issuer servicing xi_b. And the person fixed effect removes selection only for the level, not for the ranking: which pair of cards a person holds is itself selected.

estimators.name: (d) Borrower-by-month fixed effects with an issuer dummy (Antoniou-Lyman-Pagel-Stewart design)
estimators.description: Same person, same month, compare cards; issuer dummy captures which card is first/more likely to go 30+ late. Target is estimand (1). Antoniou et al. SSRN 5121519 use borrower-by-billing-cycle fixed effects on UK FCA-linked multi-card data (https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5121519).
estimators.why: Proven by logic: the third channel enters delinquency through Liq_it, which is indexed by (i,t) only, and any (i,t)-only term is absorbed exactly by borrower-by-month fixed effects. Free riding changes WHO is in stress, not which of a stressed person's cards goes first. So the user's claim that free riding 'harms the ability to come up with a payment hierarchy estimator' is false for this estimator. One residual: if the badge-induced line lands on a specific other card k, that card's utilization falls, and Andersson-Chomsisengphet-Glennon-Li (JMCB 2013, https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/jmoncb/v45y2013i2-3p251-275.html) document that available credit shifts the pecking order. That is a card-level utilization effect (kappa term), not a person-level one, and it is small relative to the person-level liquidity effect; it can be tested by adding card utilization as in (e).
estimators.what_remains_confounded: The issuer dummy is NOT the brand effect (2). It equals pi_b + xi_b + product-feature differences (line size, pay-in-full charge card, APR, rewards, autopay enrolment, due-date placement, collections outreach) + balance-share term rho (Gathergood et al. balance matching means the card carrying more balance gets more of the payment). Also: Antoniou et al. condition on cards that are delinquent in the same month, which is selection on the outcome; hierarchy needs the FIRST-to-30+ event in a month when the person is current on the others. And the sample is people who hold both a premium and a non-premium card, so the estimate is a LATE for the co-holding population, which is exactly the population where selection on eta was strong enough to get them the Amex.

estimators.name: (e) Same design adding card line and balance controls
estimators.description: Borrower-by-month FE plus card line, balance, utilization, APR as regressors, issuer dummy retained.
estimators.why: Free riding itself does not bias it (person-level liquidity already absorbed). But line and balance are POST-TREATMENT: line L_j is set by the issuer from f_i, eta_ib, G_i and other lenders' lines (line endogeneity); balance is chosen by the borrower under balance matching. Controlling for them (i) conditions on a collider: L_j depends on the issuer's private signal eta_ib, and D_ijt depends on eta_ib through theta, so within-person the issuer dummy picks up the part of eta that the line 'reveals'; (ii) blocks the part of pi_b that operates through the line the issuer chose to give. The result is a legitimate but DIFFERENT estimand: 'pure label/priority effect holding the card's terms fixed', not the hierarchy as borrowers actually face it. Report both (d) and (e); the gap between them is the line/balance mediation.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Issuer servicing xi_b, product type, and the collider through eta_ib. Line and balance controls do not remove selection into holding the pair.

estimators.name: (f) Regression discontinuity at the premium issuer's approval cutoff, outcome = repayment on OTHER lenders' accounts
estimators.description: Compare applicants just above vs just below the Amex approval threshold; outcomes measured on their non-Amex tradelines over the next 12-24 months. This is the LPP design with the badge sign reversed.
estimators.why: This does not suffer from the third channel; it MEASURES it. The RD gives the causal effect of getting the badge on other-lender delinquency for the marginal applicant. But that effect bundles three things: (i) the Amex line itself adds liquidity and lowers total utilization (mechanical, would happen with any lender), (ii) other lenders' lines respond to the lender NAME (the free-riding coefficient lam_G proper), (iii) balances migrate to the new card. To isolate (ii), run the other lenders' LINES as the intermediate outcome and compare against a non-premium lender's cutoff RD with a similar line size, or a same-size line from a lender whose name is neutral. Caveats: Amex has no single public score cutoff (multi-attribute model), so this needs issuer-internal application data or a bureau-observed inquiry-plus-booking proxy; the LATE is for near-cutoff applicants (roughly FICO 660-700, not the > 740 core), and LPP's 2016 working paper found the MARGINAL payday applicant's score was NOT affected while the average applicant's was, so a marginal-applicant RD may understate the badge effect for the typical holder.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Direct liquidity of the new line vs identity signal, unless the design has a non-premium comparison RD. Nothing about hierarchy (1); this is a person-level outcome.

estimators.name: (g) Portfolio-transfer event study (same accounts, new issuer brand)
estimators.description: Accounts sold from issuer X to issuer Y (e.g. Costco co-brand from Amex to Citi, 2016); compare delinquency before vs after on the same accounts, against a control portfolio. Target is estimand (2).
estimators.why: Proven by logic from the DGP: at transfer the bureau tradeline's lender name changes, so every other lender's model re-reads the file; if lam_G differs between the old and new name, other lenders' lines move, Liq_it moves, and delinquency on the transferred accounts moves for a reason that is not the brand effect on those accounts. The event study attributes that to the new brand. Fix: observe the same people's OTHER tradelines and lines around the transfer date (bureau archive) and net them out, or show they did not move.
estimators.what_remains_confounded: Even with lam_G = 0: the new issuer re-underwrites lines, changes APR/terms and rewards (Costco: the product changed, not only the plastic), changes servicing and collections (xi_b), and triggers attrition (people who leave are selected). The transfer date is one calendar date, so it co-moves with macro conditions; needs a control portfolio. Brand effect estimated this way = label + terms + servicing, not separable.

formal.claim_verdict:
PARTLY TRUE, and the true part is not about the hierarchy estimator.

TRUE (a: by logic, b: with published support for the mechanism): (1) Lenders do read tradeline identity: FICO reason code 06 penalizes consumer-finance accounts with no payment information (https://www.trudiligence.com/docs/ficoscorefactors.pdf), and Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania show a UK payday tradeline cut scores ~4.7% at once and ~10% after four quarters and reduced future bank credit with no worse repayment in the application quarter (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304405X21003299; 2016 WP numbers at https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/100_Liberman_HighCostCreditAndBorrowerReputation....pdf). (2) If a premium badge has the mirror-image effect, the person's total liquidity depends on who lent to them, and liquidity moves delinquency on every card (ACMS QJE 2018 numbers above). (3) Therefore every estimator that compares ACROSS PEOPLE is contaminated: the pool comparison (a), the with/without-Amex cross-section (b), the portfolio transfer (g), and the abs-risk 'selection vs priority' decomposition. The 'selection' residual in abs-risk contains badge-induced liquidity, which is neither selection nor priority. (4) Card lines are jointly determined across issuers, so 'line' is not a pre-treatment control; conditioning on it changes the estimand.

FALSE / OVERSTATED: (1) Free riding does NOT bias the payment-hierarchy estimator proper, i.e. the within-person, within-month first-to-30+ comparison (d). The third channel is a person-month scalar and is absorbed exactly by borrower-by-month fixed effects. What blocks a hierarchy estimator is data access (same-person cross-issuer monthly DPD exists only in Argus/TransUnion consortium data, the UK FCA-linked panel, or bureau archives), plus the fact that an issuer dummy is not a brand effect (product terms and servicing ride along). (2) 'Priority vs selection' in the abs-risk sense was already unidentified before free riding enters; free riding adds a third unidentified component, it does not create the problem. (3) MAGNITUDE is unmeasured for a positive badge (c: plausible, no number). The only published sign is for a negative badge. And the published own-line elasticity says a $1,000 line increase moves 4-year 90+ DPD by about 1.16 pp for FICO <= 660 and about zero for FICO > 740 (https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf). Since the Amex book is mostly > 740, the liquidity leg of the third channel is likely small for the population where Amex's entry advantage lives; if so the channel cannot explain much of the 0.29x entry ratio. That is an extrapolation from own-card lines to other-card lines and is not proven.

Bottom line for the committee: keep the hierarchy estimator (d) with a first-to-30+ event definition; stop reading pool-level entry/conversion gaps as 'selection'; treat lines as outcomes; and go measure lam_G before claiming the third channel matters.
formal.third_channel_statement: Precise statement: holding a premium tradeline (G_i = 1) changes the credit lines other issuers assign to the same person (L_k = ... + lam_G*G_i + ..., lam_G > 0 if the name is read as a positive signal, in the way that consumer-finance names are read as negative under FICO reason code 06 and payday names were read as negative in Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania). Those lines change the person's total available credit Liq_it = cash + sum_k (L_k - B_k), and for subprime holders also their balances (MPB 0.59 per $1 at FICO <= 660, Agarwal et al. QJE 2018). Liq_it and utilization then enter the delinquency index of EVERY card the person holds, with a net sign that is negative (fewer delinquencies) for prime and positive for subprime. Where it enters the estimators: it is a person-month term, so it (i) shifts the level of delinquency for badge holders vs non-holders in any cross-person comparison (pool trust comparison, with/without-Amex cross-section, portfolio transfer, and the abs-risk entry/conversion decomposition), where it is indistinguishable from selection; (ii) is absorbed and therefore harmless in borrower-by-month fixed-effects hierarchy estimators, except for a small residual via the utilization of the specific cards whose lines moved (the Andersson et al. 'available credit shifts the pecking order' effect); (iii) is the very quantity an approval-cutoff RD with other-lender outcomes measures. Status: mechanism is (b) supported with numbers for a negative badge; existence and size for a positive premium badge is (c) plausible, unmeasured.
formal.line_endogeneity_statement: Each issuer's line is a function of the bureau file, and the bureau file contains the other issuers' lines and names: L_j = lam0 + lam_f f_i + lam_G G_i + lam_L sum_{k != j} L_k + lam_eta eta_ib + e_j for every j, so the line vector solves L = (I - Lam)^{-1}(lam_f f_i + lam_G G_i + lam_eta eta + e). Three consequences, all by logic: (1) a card's line is a post-treatment outcome of every lender's reading of the file, including the premium badge, not a pre-treatment characteristic of the borrower; (2) 'same line, different issuer' comparisons compare different people, because two issuers give the same line to people with different (f, eta, G, other-lines) vectors; (3) putting the line in a delinquency regression conditions on a variable that carries the issuer's private signal eta_ib (a collider between issuer identity and delinquency) and blocks the part of any brand or priority effect that runs through the line the issuer chose. Evidence that issuers condition on total exposure and utilization is standard model practice (bureau attributes such as total revolving limit and aggregate utilization are in every prime card model; FICO reason codes on 'proportion of balances to credit limits' exist in the same list as code 06). The sign of lam_L is ambiguous: positive when total limits are read as capacity, negative when the issuer caps its share of wallet. Magnitude of lam_L for U.S. card issuers: not published; unknown.
formal.what_would_prove_magnitude:
The third channel's size is lam_G (badge -> other lenders' lines) times the delinquency response to those lines, summed over the person's cards. Measure the two legs separately.

Leg 1, lam_G (the free-riding coefficient). Three designs, best first:
 (i) Own-model counterfactual (cleanest, available to any issuer now): take the issuer's live underwriting/line-assignment model and the prescreen criteria, score the applicant population once as is and once with lender-identity attributes (lender name, 'premium card present', consumer-finance-account counts) neutralized, and record the change in approval and assigned line by FICO band. That is lam_G for that issuer's model by construction. Repeat across the Y-14M reporters through the regulator if a market-wide number is wanted. No bias question arises.
 (ii) Approval-cutoff RD at the premium issuer (needs Amex-internal application scores, or a bureau-observed inquiry-plus-booking proxy), outcome = other lenders' credit lines and new-account openings at 6, 12, 24 months, split by FICO band. Compare with the same RD at a non-premium issuer of similar line size to separate lender-name reading from the mechanical utilization/score effect of any new line. LATE at the cutoff only.
 (iii) Portfolio transfers where a premium name replaces a non-premium one (or the reverse), with the bureau archive showing the same people's other-lender lines before and after the name change; control portfolio for calendar effects.

Leg 2, delinquency response to other-lender lines by FICO. Already partly published for OWN-card lines: $1,000 raises 4-year 90+ DPD by 1.16 pp at FICO <= 660, ~0 at > 740, from 743 credit-limit RDs on 8.5 million accounts (https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf). What is missing is the cross-card version: the effect of a line increase on card k on delinquency of card j != k, same person. Data for that: a bureau research panel or Argus/TransUnion consortium data with lender identity, lines, balances and monthly DPD for all of a person's cards (the NY Fed CCP/Equifax panel has lines and DPD but not lender name; Y-14M has one issuer's accounts with bureau aggregates but not other lenders' individual lines). Design: issuer k's line RDs (ACMS style) with outcomes measured on the person's other tradelines.

Combine: third-channel effect on entry rate = lam_G(FICO) x [sum over other cards of dD/dL(FICO)] x line-dollars per badge, computed by FICO band and weighted by the Amex book's FICO mix. Compare that number with the observed entry gap (Amex 30+ share 0.29x Synchrony in abs-risk). If lam_G is a few thousand dollars and the > 740 cross-card elasticity is near zero, the channel is immaterial for the Amex-vs-Synchrony question and the memo can say so with numbers; if the cross-card elasticity for prime is not zero, it is material. Until Leg 1 is measured the claim stays 'plausible, unmeasured'.
key_assumptions: Delinquency on each card depends on the person's TOTAL liquidity (sum of available credit across lenders plus cash), not only on that card's own line. Supported in sign by Andersson et al. 2013 (available credit shifts mortgage-vs-card default order) and ACMS 2018 (own-line effects by FICO); the cross-card elasticity is not published.

The free-riding coefficient lam_G is nonzero and positive for a premium badge. Only the negative-badge case (payday, consumer-finance accounts) has published evidence; the positive case is assumed by analogy.

The third channel operates through person-month quantities (total liquidity, total balance) and not through a card-specific mechanism other than utilization; this is what makes borrower-by-month fixed effects absorb it.

Selection on the issuer's private signal eta is on the LEVEL of creditworthiness, not on the person's ranking of cards; if Amex selected people who specifically protect Amex (selection on pi), then (d) would also be contaminated by selection into the co-holding sample.
Hierarchy is defined on the first-to-30+ event among cards that were current, not on the set of cards already delinquent in the same month (Antoniou et al. condition on the latter).
The abs-risk trust pools are treated as if they had the same FICO mix; 10-D data contain no FICO, so 'at constant FICO' is assumed, not observed.
Issuer servicing (xi_b: hardship programs, re-aging, outreach, charge-off timing) is not separately measured and is bundled into every issuer contrast including the conversion ratio.
The ACMS own-line elasticities (1.16 pp per $1,000 at <= 660, ~0 at > 740, 4-year 90+ DPD) are used as a stand-in for the cross-card elasticity when sizing the channel; this is an extrapolation.
Line endogeneity is linear and stable across issuers (lam_L constant); in practice each issuer's model reads total limits and utilization differently and the sign of lam_L is unknown.

Portfolio-transfer events change only the lender name on the bureau file; in the known cases (Costco Amex to Citi, 2016) product terms also changed, so that design overstates the brand effect unless terms are held fixed.

refutation.strongest_objection:
The formalization's central "proven by logic" claims rest on a sign assumption its own sources do not support, and the one published study that measured the whole chain found the last link close to zero.

The delinquency equation has beta(f) >= 0 with "larger for prime", so that extra other-lender credit lowers delinquency for Amex-type holders and the third channel makes Amex "look more selected than it is". The cited evidence says the opposite or nothing: ACMS (https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jstroebe/PDF/ACMS_Passthrough.pdf) finds a $1,000 limit increase raises 4-year 90+ DPD by 1.16 pp on a 14.5% base at FICO <= 660 and is "close to zero" for the > 740 group, and $1 of limit adds +3.7 cents of charge-offs even at > 740. No source in the formalization shows that more available credit LOWERS delinquency for any FICO band; the negative-for-prime sign is invented. Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania is the only study that observed badge -> other lenders' credit -> repayment end to end: the payday tradeline cut scores (-4.7% same quarter, -10% at four quarters) and cut future bank credit, and the JFE 2021 abstract (search snippet from https://www.fmg.ac.uk/fre/publications/academic-journals/high-cost-debt-and-perceived-creditworthiness-evidence-uk; ScienceDirect/SSRN 403 from this machine) says this "does not affect future debt repayment"; the 2016 working paper abstract says the opposite ("more default ... in the future", https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/100_Liberman_HighCostCreditAndBorrowerReputation....pdf). Either way the published measured effect of the credit change on repayment is zero or of contested sign, and for the marginal (RD) applicant, which is exactly the design the formalization recommends in (f), LPP found no score change, no rationing and no repayment change at all. So: the direction of the third channel's contamination in the trust comparison is unknown, not "makes Amex look more selected"; under the ACMS sign a negative store-card badge would REDUCE Synchrony's delinquency and the 0.29x would understate the gap, under the LPP working-paper sign the reverse. A bias whose sign is unknown and whose best measured magnitude is near zero for the prime population where Amex's advantage lives cannot be labelled "proven by logic".
errors_found: SIGN: model asserts beta(f) larger for prime and a negative net line effect for prime; ACMS shows the delinquency effect is ~0 at > 740 and the charge-off effect is +3.7 cents per $1 (positive). Two cited papers disagree on the subprime sign (ACMS: more credit -> more delinquency; LPP 2016 WP: less credit -> more default). The 'sign by FICO' table is asserted, not sourced.

MIS-STATED EVIDENCE: 'no worse repayment' is attributed to LPP as if settled. The 2016 WP abstract says the average applicant has 'more default and credit rationing ... in the future'; the -11% default figure is same-quarter and not significant; the JFE 2021 abstract (per search snippet, unverified verbatim) says no effect on future repayment. The two versions disagree and the formalization reports only the version that helps the mechanism while omitting that LPP is a measured near-null on the channel's final link.

MIS-ATTRIBUTED DESIGN: estimator (d) is described as the 'Antoniou-Lyman-Pagel-Stewart design' with an issuer dummy capturing which card goes late first. Their paper (AEA 2026 PDF) tests opportunistic borrowing: sample = borrowers newly delinquent on several cards in the same month; outcome = net borrowing/repayment on cards eventually charged off vs not; no issuer dummy, no first-to-30+ ordering, UK 2013-14 data from 5 issuers. (d) is the author's own proposal and has no published instance.

ABSORPTION OVERSTATED: 'absorbed exactly by borrower-by-month FE, proven by logic' holds only because Liq_it enters the latent index additively with the SAME coefficient beta(f_i) on every card. If the liquidity coefficient differs by card (high minimum payment, card used for essentials, charge card that must be paid in full), Liq_it x beta_j is not absorbed. Andersson et al. 2013 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/jmoncb/v45y2013i2-3p251-275.html) is cited as support yet shows precisely that person-level available credit changes the ORDER between products, i.e. it does not drop out of the ranking.

CARD-LEVEL LEG CALLED 'SMALL' WITHOUT A NUMBER: the author's own DGP puts the badge-induced line on specific cards k (kappa*util, rho*share, B = m(f)*L with m = 0.59 at <= 660 per ACMS). For subprime the whole ACMS line effect runs through balances, which is card-level, so the unabsorbed part is the main part for that population, not a residual.

ESTIMAND CONFUSION (a)/(b): estimand (3) is defined as a descriptive difference in means between different people that 'is not a causal effect of anything', then its estimator is declared 'biased by free riding'. A difference in means is not biased by one of its own components; the correct statement is that the abs-risk INTERPRETATION of the gap as selection is unidentified, which the prior review already established. Free riding names one more component of an already unidentified residual; it creates no new bias.

ESTIMAND CONFUSION (g): estimand (2) is defined 'with all of i's other accounts held fixed', which excludes the third channel by construction; the 'bias' in the portfolio-transfer event study is then a mismatch between estimator and an arbitrarily narrow estimand. Under the equally natural total-effect definition (brand including how other lenders read it) the same estimator is unbiased for that part. 'Biased' depends on an unstated estimand choice.

COLLIDER MIS-STATED in (e): within person, eta_ib affects D only through theta, which alpha_i (or the borrower-month FE) absorbs, so L_j is a mediator of issuer identity, not a collider between issuer and D. The correct point (controlling for line changes the estimand by blocking the mediated path) is already made separately; the collider claim needs card-specific private information in eta_ib, which the model does not contain.

IDENTITY VS CLASS: the evidence that lenders 'read lender identity' is FICO reason code 06 (consumer finance company ACCOUNT TYPE) and LPP (payday PRODUCT TYPE). Neither shows that a specific bank name is read. Amex vs Synchrony differ in account class (bankcard vs retail/private label), which is bundled with line size and use; Amex -> Citi (Costco) is a bankcard-to-bankcard transfer with no class change, so lam_G for that event study is plausibly ~0 in the very example given.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION: estimator (a) is 'biased ... proven by logic ... makes Amex look MORE selected', while FALSE/OVERSTATED (3) concedes the liquidity leg is 'likely small' for > 740 and 'cannot explain much of the 0.29x'. Both cannot stand as written.

ESTIMAND (1) DRIFT: H is averaged over 'multi-card holders in stress'. Free riding changes who is in stress (the author concedes this); if pi_b, rho, kappa are heterogeneous across people, the population-average hierarchy moves with lam_G. This is estimand instability, not estimator bias, and the write-up does not separate the two.

MINOR: 10-D trust pools are securitized subsets of eligible receivables, not the issuer's book, so even a FICO-matched comparison would compare selected sub-portfolios; the formalization treats pool = book.
refutation.what_survives: (a) By logic: the three estimands are distinct and the abs-risk conclusions page ("selection, and it is not close", 0.29x entry share, 1.38x conversion, C:/Users/samwe/code/abs-risk/docs/conclusions.html) is an estimand-(3) descriptive gap that cannot be read as selection, priority, or brand; the prior review's point that entry fits both stories stands, and the conversion ratio conditions on a post-treatment event and is consistent with priority as well as selection. (a) By logic: card lines are jointly determined across issuers from the bureau file, so a line is an outcome, not a pre-treatment control, and putting it in a delinquency regression changes the estimand. (b) With numbers: score models and other lenders do respond to the TYPE of tradeline on the file, independent of repayment: FICO reason code 06 (https://www.trudiligence.com/docs/ficoscorefactors.pdf) and LPP's -4.7%/-10% score effect with less future bank credit and no worse same-quarter repayment (https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/100_Liberman_HighCostCreditAndBorrowerReputation....pdf). (b) With numbers: own-card line changes move delinquency for subprime (1.16 pp per $1,000 at <= 660) and not for prime (ACMS). (a) By logic: the person-month part of any liquidity effect, entering with a common coefficient across cards, is absorbed by borrower-by-month fixed effects, so a within-person within-month first-to-30+ estimator is protected against that part. (c) Plausible, unmeasured: a positive premium badge raises other lenders' lines (lam_G > 0); no published number. The proposed Leg 1(i) measurement (re-score the applicant population with identity/type attributes neutralized) is sound and is the cheapest way to settle lam_G.
refutation.corrected_verdict:
The user's claim ("free riding harms the ability to come up with a payment hierarchy estimator") is NOT established, and the formalization's "PARTLY TRUE" verdict is overstated in both directions.

What can be said: (1) Cross-person comparisons (trust pools, with/without-Amex cross-sections, portfolio transfers) were already unable to attribute the Amex-Synchrony entry gap to selection; free riding adds one more unidentified term with UNKNOWN sign and, on the only measured evidence, small size for prime borrowers (ACMS: ~0 delinquency effect at > 740; LPP: the change in other lenders' credit did not change future repayment per the JFE abstract, or raised default per the 2016 WP). The abs-risk sentence "selection, and it is not close" should be withdrawn on the prior review's grounds, not on free-riding grounds. (2) A within-person, within-month first-to-30+ estimator is protected against the person-level part of the channel only under the common-coefficient assumption; the card-level part (badge-induced line on a specific card changing its utilization and balance share, which for subprime is the main part per ACMS's 0.59 MPB) is not absorbed and is not a nuisance: it changes the hierarchy itself. So the right statement is that the hierarchy is an equilibrium object that depends on every lender's line-setting, which limits its use for issuer-specific counterfactuals, rather than that the estimator is biased. (3) No published instance of that estimator exists; Antoniou et al. is a different design (synchronous delinquents, charged-off vs not, no issuer term) and should not be cited as it. (4) The evidence that lenders read a tradeline is about account CLASS (consumer finance, payday), not bank NAME; the Amex-vs-Synchrony case is a bankcard-vs-retail class difference bundled with product terms, and a bankcard-to-bankcard transfer (Costco) likely carries no free-riding change at all. (5) Magnitude for a positive badge: unknown; measure lam_G by re-scoring with identity/type attributes neutralized before any claim that the channel matters.
