evidence.summary: LINK 1 (lenders and scores read the TYPE or LABEL of other tradelines and change credit supply) is supported by published evidence with numbers at the level of lender TYPE and file LABELS, and is unmeasured at the level of a premium BRAND. Proven by documentation: FICO reason codes explicitly penalize consumer-finance-company accounts (code 06 and related codes A8/B1/J2/99) and reward bank/national revolving history (F5, J1, G2), and bureau files carry a machine-readable industry code per tradeline (Experian KOB: BB, BC, FP, FZ), so lender type is an input, not just a by-product. Supported with numbers: (1) Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania (UK, 51,355 applicants): taking a payday loan cuts the credit score 4.7% in the same quarter while same-quarter default falls ~11% (n.s.) and debt-collection searches fall 16%; the effect vanishes for already-low-score applicants, so it is the label, not repayment. (2) Foley-Hurtado-Liberman-Sepulveda (Chile): when a retailer's card book was sold to a bank and 1.8M good-standing borrowers became visible in the bank registry, OTHER banks raised those borrowers' limits by ~156,000 pesos (~$310, 6.7% of a 2.3M-peso mean) within three quarters, concentrated among borrowers whose predicted default fell; this is the clearest published case of one lender's tradeline raising other lenders' lines in the positive direction. (3) Dobbie et al. (US, Equifax 5% sample): removing a bankruptcy flag adds 10 score points and +$1,510 (about +50%) in card limits over 3 years. (4) Musto 2004: flag removal roughly doubled lines for medium/high-rated consumers. (5) Hertzberg-Liberti-Paravisini (Argentina firms): making one lender's poor rating public cut that lender's own credit 19.8% and raised distress 5.6pp. Industry practice: Chase 5/24 counts new cards from ALL issuers (negative direction); Amex 2/90 and 1/5 count only Amex cards; OCC handbook confirms prescreen tiers and line assignment use bureau score plus criteria level and that scores weigh "types of credit available". Important caveat for the US: Bhutta (FEDS 2013-81) and Bhutta-Skiba-Tobacman (JMCB 2015) show US payday loans are generally NOT reported to Equifax/Experian/TransUnion and have near-zero score effects (-1.14 points, SE 1.37), so the UK stigma result does not transfer to US payday tradelines. Not found anywhere: a study showing that an Amex/Chase Sapphire tradeline raises approvals or lines elsewhere, or a US study showing one issuer's line increase causes other issuers to raise lines (Agarwal et al. QJE 2018, Aydin AER 2022 and Bord-Kovacs-Moran 2026 do not test it). Net: the "free-riding" mechanism is real and sized for labels and lender types (effects of 5% to 100% on lines depending on the label), but the brand-specific link needed for the user's third channel is (c) plausible but unmeasured.

findings.claim: FICO scoring explicitly reads lender TYPE: multiple reason codes penalize consumer-finance-company accounts and treat bank/national revolving vs retail vs sales-finance accounts differently.
findings.evidence: The FICO reason code list (2013 Fair Isaac document) contains: 'Amount owed on recently opened consumer finance company accounts is too high' (A8 / code 55), 'Lack of recent consumer finance company account information' (code 99), 'Length of time consumer finance company loans have been established' (J2 / 25), 'Amount owed on recently opened sales finance company accounts is too high' (B1 / 98), plus bank/national revolving codes ('Lack of recent bank/national revolving information' F5; 'Length of time bank/national revolving accounts have been established' J1 / 14; 'No recent bank/national revolving balances' G2) and retail codes (A9 / 40, F8, J5 / 12). Code 06 'Too many consumer finance company accounts' is documented across myFICO forum threads and consumer-education sites. Presence of a consumer finance account lowers the score even after closure. Magnitude in points is not published by FICO.
findings.numbers: Point magnitudes: unknown (FICO does not publish weights). Codes verified: 06, A8/55, 99, J2/25, B1/98, F5, J1/14, G2, A9/40, F8, J5/12.
findings.source_title: US FICO Score Reason Codes (Fair Isaac, 2013); myFICO forum 'Too many consumer finance company accounts'

findings.claim: Bureau files carry a machine-readable industry/lender-type code on every tradeline, so lender type (and often lender name) is available to any custom model or prescreen.
findings.evidence: Experian Credit Profile Report guides list Kind-of-Business (KOB) codes attached to each tradeline: BB (all banks nonspecific), BC (bank credit cards), BM (bank mortgage), BI (bank installment), FP (personal loan companies), FZ (finance companies nonspecific). The creditor name also appears on the tradeline. This proves the input exists; it does not by itself show how any lender uses it.
findings.numbers: n/a (format documentation)
findings.source_title: How to read an Experian Credit Profile Report (700Credit)

findings.claim: A high-cost (payday) tradeline lowers other lenders' assessment and future credit even though repayment does not worsen (UK).
findings.evidence: Liberman, Paravisini and Pathania use quasi-random loan-officer assignment at a UK high-cost lender (51,355 first-time applicants, credit bureau quarterly snapshots). Loan take-up reduces the credit score of the average borrower by 4.7% within the quarter of application; in that same quarter default propensity falls ~11% (not significant) and debt-collection searches fall 16% (10% level), so the score drop is not driven by repayment. Borrowers then increase credit-search intensity without gaining credit (rationing by standard lenders). An RD at the lender's own score-eligibility threshold (take-up jumps ~25pp) shows NO score effect for very-low-score applicants, consistent with a reputation/label mechanism. Published JFE 142(2) 2021, 719-736.
findings.numbers: Score -4.7% same quarter; default -11% (n.s.); collection searches -16%; take-up jump at threshold ~25pp; N=51,355; average loan £288, APR >700%.
findings.source_title: High-Cost Debt and Borrower Reputation: Evidence from the U.K. (CFPB research conference version); JFE 2021

findings.claim: When one lender's good-standing tradelines become visible to other banks, other banks raise those borrowers' credit limits (positive-direction spillover through the registry).
findings.evidence: Foley, Hurtado, Liberman and Sepulveda (Dec 2018 working paper) use a 10% sample of the Chilean regulator's individual-by-lender card data (849,449 individuals, 23 lenders). A retailer card portfolio was sold to a bank in May 2015, making 1.8 million previously invisible non-defaulting borrowers observable in the bank credit registry (bank cards +30%). Difference-in-differences vs other retailers' borrowers: three quarters after the sale, bank-issued limits for the Lender's borrowers rose 156,000 pesos (~$310), a 6.7% increase on the 2.3M-peso pre-mean, with parallel pre-trends. Increases were larger for borrowers whose predicted default probability fell once their history was revealed. The Lender itself raised its own borrowers' limits by ~260,000 pesos (30%). Short-run usage of the new credit was small. Note: this reveals repayment history and the existence of the account, not brand per se.
findings.numbers: Other-bank limits +156,000 CLP (~$310) = +6.7% after 3 quarters; own-lender limits +260,000 CLP (+30%); 1.8M borrowers affected; new borrowers' origination limits doubled.
findings.source_title: The Effects of Information on Credit Market Competition: Evidence from Credit Cards (AEA 2019 preliminary)

findings.claim: US card lenders react to a file LABEL (bankruptcy flag) with large limit changes, independent of repayment behavior.
findings.evidence: Dobbie, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Mahoney and Song (J. Finance 2020) compare Chapter 13 filers (flag removed at 7 years) with Chapter 7 filers (10 years) in the Equifax CCP 5% sample. Flag removal produces an immediate 10-point score increase (pre-mean 596), a 3pp fall in implied default probability (from 32%), and over three years credit limits rise by about one-half ($1,510 on a $3,027 mean) and card balances by >40% ($800 on $1,911); the share with a mortgage rises 1.9pp in year one. Labor market effects are zero.
findings.numbers: Score +10 pts; limits +$1,510 (+50%) at 3 years; balances +$800 (+40%); mortgage share +1.9pp.
findings.source_title: Bad Credit, No Problem? Credit and Labor Market Consequences of Bad Credit Reports (NY Fed Staff Report 795 / JF 2020)

findings.claim: Earlier US evidence: removing the bankruptcy flag roughly doubles credit lines for medium- and high-rated consumers.
findings.evidence: Musto (2004, Journal of Business) documents average credit lines of about $215 (low rating) before and $600 after flag removal, and for medium/high ratings roughly $800 and $2,000 before rising to about $2,810 and $4,578 in the removal year (figures as summarized in the Applied Economics 2010 follow-up abstract; original JSTOR article not opened).
findings.source_title: What Happens When Information Leaves a Market? Evidence from Postbankruptcy Consumers (Musto 2004), via ideas.repec summary

findings.claim: Lenders act on OTHER lenders' assessments once those become public, and anticipate each other's reactions (corporate evidence).
findings.evidence: Hertzberg, Liberti and Paravisini (J. Finance 2011) exploit Argentina's 1998 public credit registry expansion (reporting threshold cut from $200,000 to $50). Comparing firms with $150-200k debt (treated) to $200-250k (control): the announcement causes a 19.8% decline in a firm's debt with lenders that had privately rated it a poor risk, before other lenders could see the rating; distress rises 5.6pp; firms with perfect records but multiple lenders see a permanent 6.9% debt decline. No effect for single-lender firms.
findings.numbers: -19.8% debt with poor-rating lenders; +5.6pp distress; -6.9% permanent for multi-lender firms with clean records.
findings.source_title: Public Information and Coordination: Evidence from a Credit Registry Expansion (Feb 2010 working paper; JF 66(2) 2011)

findings.claim: Information sharing changes where borrowers get credit and how much even when lender IDENTITY is hidden (so identity is not necessary for spillovers).
findings.evidence: Sutherland (JAE 2018) uses PayNet equipment-finance credit files, where lenders are anonymous in the shared file (Jackson 2000 cited). When a firm's file becomes shared, it is 6.9% more likely to switch lenders and 6.1% more likely to exit a relationship (vs 29% unconditional two-year exit), thin-file firms see an 8.1% decline in credit in the shared relationship, and new-relationship formation rises 5.8%; lenders become less willing to renew with delinquent borrowers.
findings.numbers: +6.9% switch; +6.1% exit vs 29% base; -8.1% credit for thin-file shared relationship; +5.8% new relationships.
findings.source_title: Does Credit Reporting Lead to a Decline in Relationship Lending? Evidence from Information Sharing Technology (MPRA 93670)

findings.claim: A registry rating downgrade caused by bad luck (not behavior) cuts a consumer's borrowing for three years (Peru).
findings.evidence: Garmaise and Natividad (J. Finance 2017) use Peruvian consumer bank loan data 2001-2011 and currency movements; a rating downgrade from bad luck causes a three-year reduction in financing, and for severely delinquent borrowers the reporting downgrade itself accounts for 25-65% of the decline in borrowing over the following years. All banks see each other's ratings in the central registry.
findings.numbers: Downgrade explains 25-65% of post-delinquency borrowing decline; effect lasts ~3 years.
findings.source_title: Consumer Default, Credit Reporting, and Borrowing Constraints

findings.claim: Shorter retention of arrears flags in Sweden raised scores and new credit access, and raised subsequent default.
findings.evidence: Bos and Nakamura (Phila Fed WP 14-21) exploit the 2003 change from year-end removal to exact three-year retention; the removal produced an abrupt, persistent score improvement and significant new credit access, while affected borrowers defaulted more often; banks tightened standards. Effect sizes not extracted (abstract only).
findings.numbers: unknown (not extracted)
findings.source_title: Should Defaults Be Forgotten? Evidence from Variation in Removal of Negative Consumer Credit Information

findings.claim: US payday tradelines are generally invisible to the big three bureaus, so the UK 'payday stigma' channel does not transfer to US payday loans; payday access has near-zero effect on scores.
findings.evidence: Bhutta (FEDS 2013-81) states payday borrowing 'is not reported to the national credit bureaus Equifax, Experian and TransUnion' and finds access to payday loans changes Equifax scores by -2.86 (cross-state) or -1.14 points (SE 1.37, state FE), i.e., zero. Bhutta, Skiba and Tobacman (JMCB 2015) RD at a payday lender's approval threshold finds long-run effects on scores 'close to zero'. Implication: a lender-type label only matters when the tradeline is reported; FICO's consumer-finance codes bite on reported finance-company accounts (retail/furniture financing, subprime auto, installment lenders), not typical storefront payday loans.
findings.numbers: Score effect -1.14 pts (SE 1.37); -2.86 pts alt spec; payday applicants avg cumulative card limit ~$3,000 and >5 inquiries.
findings.source_title: Payday Loans and Consumer Financial Health (Bhutta, FEDS 2013-81); Payday Loan Choices and Consequences (JMCB 2015)

findings.claim: Card issuers read the count and recency of OTHER issuers' tradelines (negative direction): Chase 5/24 denies applicants with 5+ new cards from any issuer in 24 months.
findings.evidence: Experian's explainer and multiple industry sources state Chase counts new personal cards from all issuers (and authorized-user accounts) on the credit report in the last 24 months. Citi's community-documented 6/6 rule rejects more than six hard inquiries in six months. By contrast Amex's 2/90 and 1/5 velocity rules and 5-card cap count only Amex cards. These are documented practice, not published policy, and they show lenders condition on cross-issuer tradeline COUNTS, not on brand.
findings.numbers: Chase: >=5 new cards / 24 months = auto-denial; Citi: >6 inquiries / 6 months; Amex: max 2 approvals / 90 days, 1 / 5 days, 5 credit cards total.
findings.source_title: What Is Chase's 5/24 Rule and How Does It Work? (Experian); Citi 8/65 rule (Doctor of Credit); Amex application rules (Bankrate)

findings.claim: Regulatory guidance confirms prescreen selection and initial line assignment run on bureau attributes and that bureau scores weigh 'types of credit available', but does not name other lenders' limits or lender identity as inputs.
findings.evidence: OCC Comptroller's Handbook, Credit Card Lending v2.0: bureau scores consider five groups including 'Types of credit available'; banks give bureaus written prescreen criteria with exclusion criteria (serious derogatories, recent bankruptcy, limited trade lines) and tiered credit criteria (A/B/C/D) built on bureau scores; line assignment is 'based on a combination of disclosed income, credit bureau score, and criteria level'; application scores 'incorporate ... various credit bureau data' and set 'pricing and initial line assignment'. The FDIC Credit Card Activities Manual chapter VII sections 'Initial Credit Line Assignments' and 'Credit Bureau Preferences' exist but the pages returned 404/403.
findings.numbers: n/a
findings.source_title: Comptroller's Handbook: Credit Card Lending (OCC)

findings.claim: Industry sources assert 'high limits beget high limits' (issuers weigh existing limits on other cards when setting a new line), but no measured effect exists.
findings.evidence: Bankrate's explainer on how issuers determine limits says issuers weigh existing limits across other cards; Amex UK's FAQ says it reviews current limits on other cards. Experian's Premier Attributes product sheet advertises 2,100+ attributes including bankcard 'available credit' concepts, but the attribute definitions (e.g., highest bankcard limit) are not public. Anecdotal, unmeasured.
findings.numbers: none
findings.source_title: How Your Credit Card Limit Is Determined (Bankrate); Experian Premier Attributes product sheet

findings.claim: Large US credit-limit studies do not test whether other lenders respond to one lender's line change; they do show low-FICO lines are costly and high-FICO borrowers shift balances across cards.
findings.evidence: Agarwal, Chomsisengphet, Mahoney and Stroebel (QJE 2018; 8.5M cards, 743 credit-limit RDs) run a placebo showing other banks' contract terms do not jump at the same FICO cutoffs, but do not estimate other lenders' limit responses. For FICO <=660, $1 of extra limit raises 4-year costs 29.6 cents (21.6 cents charge-offs); for >740, 6.0 cents (3.7 charge-offs). The >740 group shows a 23% MPB on the treated card but ~0 across all accounts (balance shifting). Aydin (AER 2022, randomized lines) reports 11 cents/dollar borrowed in Q1 and 28 cents by year 3; abstract silent on other banks. Bord, Kovacs and Moran (FEDS Note Jan 2026, Y-14M): ~12% of cards get increases yearly ($160B), 80% bank-initiated, balances rise ~30% of the increase within 6 months; no cross-lender analysis.
findings.numbers: Charge-off cost per $1 limit: 21.6c (<=660) vs 3.7c (>740); MPB >740 group 23% on card, ~0 total; Aydin 11c/28c; Bord: 30% of CLI drawn in 6 months.
findings.source_title: Do Banks Pass Through Credit Expansions to Consumers Who Want to Borrow? (working paper); Aydin AER 2022; FEDS Note 2026

gaps: No published study isolates lender BRAND (Amex, Chase Sapphire) as opposed to lender TYPE or account existence. The Chile portfolio-sale paper is the closest analogue (retailer-to-bank regime change), and it identifies visibility of repayment history, not a prestige signal.

No US evidence that one issuer's credit-limit increase causes OTHER issuers to raise limits. Agarwal et al. (QJE 2018), Aydin (AER 2022) and Bord-Kovacs-Moran (2026) do not estimate other lenders' limit responses; the Chile paper is the only causal estimate found (+6.7% after 3 quarters) and it is for a visibility shock, not a line-size shock.

A search summary claimed 'banks without links to stores reduce credit card limits by 24-51% in the year after a new card is issued'; the cited FDIC poster (Gorostiaga) is about syndicated corporate loans and does not contain this; the source of the 24-51% figure could not be found.
FDIC Credit Card Activities Manual chapter VII sections 'Initial Credit Line Assignments' and 'Credit Bureau Preferences' could not be opened (404 on the HTML, 403 on the PDF).

Experian Premier Attributes / Equifax attribute definitions (e.g., highest bankcard limit, count of bankcard trades, finance-company trades) are not public; only marketing product sheets were found, so the exact attributes used in prescreen and line assignment remain unknown.

FICO does not publish point weights for the consumer-finance-company codes; magnitude of the penalty is unknown. Whether FICO or VantageScore uses creditor NAME beyond industry type could not be confirmed either way; the VantageScore consumer page listed only a 'bankcard or revolving' code.

Hertzberg-Liberti-Paravisini numbers come from the Feb 2010 working paper, not the JF 2011 final; Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania numbers come from the CFPB conference version, not the JFE 2021 final (ScienceDirect and SSRN returned 403).
Bos-Nakamura (Sweden) effect sizes were not extracted (abstract only). Bhutta-Skiba-Tobacman (JMCB 2015) full numbers not extracted beyond 'close to zero'.

The reasonable but untested inference that an Amex tradeline raises other lenders' lines (link 1 in the positive direction for prime brands) rests only on industry anecdote ('high limits beget high limits'); no measured effect size exists.

evidence.summary:
LINK 2 = "a change in a person's credit access at OTHER lenders changes repayment on a given card." Verdict by kind of evidence:

(a) Proven by logic: the channel exists. Credit limits move total household borrowing (not just balance shifting) for anyone who is credit-constrained, and utilization is a scoring input, so any lender's line decision mechanically enters every other lender's next decision. Nobody disputes this.

(b) Supported by published numbers, split by FICO:
- SUBPRIME / NEAR-PRIME (FICO <=700): SIGN IS POSITIVE for own-card default and mixed for other debts. Agarwal-Chomsisengphet-Mahoney-Stroebel (QJE 2018, 743 credit-limit RDs, 8.5M cards): $1 more limit raises total balances across ALL cards by 59 cents at 12 months for FICO<=660 (46 cents for 661-700), i.e. it is new debt, not shifting; a $1,000 limit increase raises 60+DPD within 4 years by +1.21pp on a 16.5% base (90+DPD +1.16pp on 14.5%) for FICO<=660, +0.86/+0.80pp for 661-700. A Chinese fintech RCT (Fu et al., JEF 2025) finds +5.7pp probability of 60+ days overdue from more credit supply. Payday access raises "difficulty paying bills" by 25% among low-income households (Melzer 2011). BUT the reverse shock cuts the other way: Cohen-Cole & Morse (Boston Fed 2009, TransUnion panel 2006-07) find a one-SD DROP in available card credit raises the chance a distressed borrower goes delinquent on the mortgage rather than the card by 25% (vs 13% for a one-SD house-price fall), and the available-credit coefficient is more than 3x larger for low-score than high-score borrowers; in absolute terms less liquidity raises delinquency on BOTH products. Elul et al. (AER P&P 2010): card utilization >80% raises the mortgage default hazard by 0.65pp/quarter even at low CLTV, up to 1.5pp/q near CLTV 100, comparable to negative equity. So for subprime, more credit elsewhere = more total debt and more own-card default, but also a liquidity cushion that delays default on other obligations; the NET across the wallet is not measured anywhere.
- PRIME (FICO >740): SIGN IS ZERO TO SLIGHTLY NEGATIVE. ACMS: 23-cent MPB on the treated card but -5 cents (n.s.) across all cards = pure balance shifting; effect of $1,000 more limit on 60+DPD at 48 months is -0.32pp (95% CI [-0.61,-0.05]) and on 90+DPD -0.17pp (n.s.). Aydin (AER 2022, RCT of 45,307 credit lines in Turkey): MPB 11 cents in quarter 1, 28 cents by year 3, "no discernible effects on delinquencies." CFPB 2022 line-decrease report: superprime/prime/near-prime consumers who lost a median 75% of their line got total card balances back to pre-cut levels within 3 quarters by using other cards or new accounts; subprime/deep subprime balances stayed depressed. Dobbie-Song (AER 2020 RCT on distressed card borrowers): immediate payment reductions (short-run liquidity) had no positive effect at all; only delayed interest write-downs helped.
- LABEL -> OTHER LENDERS' SUPPLY step (the first half of the third channel) is well measured, but only for NEGATIVE labels: a UK high-cost loan cuts the credit score 4.7% in the same quarter and 10% after four quarters with repayment unchanged or better in the short run, leads to credit rationing by banks and higher default a year later, and the RD marginal applicant whose score does not move shows neither (Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania, JFE 2021). Removing a Chapter 13 flag raises card limits by about $1,510 (about 50%) and balances by $800 (40%) within 3 years (Dobbie et al., JF 2020). Shortening Sweden's arrears-flag retention led banks to tighten yet borrowers got more net credit and defaulted more often, with no rise in total defaults (Bos-Nakamura). No paper measures the effect of a POSITIVE brand label (an Amex or Chase tradeline) on other lenders' lines.

(c) Plausible but unmeasured: the exact object the user needs, delinquency on card B caused by an exogenous line change at lender A, does not appear in any paper found; ACMS come closest but report delinquency only on the treated card. Bord-Kovacs-Moran (Fed FEDS 2025-088, Y-14M) show the VOLUME of this channel is concentrated at the bottom: 60% of subprime revolving balances vs 12% of superprime balances are supported by post-origination limit increases, subprime limits grow from $700 to $2,700 in five years, and 30% of each increase becomes new revolving balance.

Implication for the Amex-vs-Synchrony question: the third channel (badge -> other lenders' lines -> liquidity -> repayment) is empirically near zero for borrowers above 740 and positive-signed (on own-card default) below 700. Because the repo compares issuers "at the same FICO," the contamination risk is real only in the shared 620-740 band, and even there its cross-card sign is not pinned down by any published estimate.

findings.claim: For FICO<=660, a $1 credit-limit increase raises total balances across ALL the borrower's cards by 59 cents at 12 months (new borrowing, not balance shifting); for >740 the treated-card MPB is 23 cents but the all-cards effect is -5 cents (not significant), i.e. pure shifting.
findings.evidence: 743 credit-limit regression discontinuities on 8.5M US credit cards merged with credit bureau data, Table V Panel C and section V.B.6.
findings.numbers: All-cards MPB at 12 months: <=660: 0.59; 661-700: 0.46; 701-740: 0.32; >740: -0.05 (n.s.). Treated-card ADB MPB: 0.58 / 0.47 / 0.43 / 0.23. Highest group holds $44,813 average total card limits.
findings.source_title: Agarwal, Chomsisengphet, Mahoney, Stroebel, Do Banks Pass Through Credit Expansions to Consumers Who Want to Borrow?, QJE 2018 (NBER w21567)
findings.direction: supports (channel is large for subprime, essentially absent for prime)

findings.claim: More credit raises delinquency on the receiving card for low and middle FICO, and has a zero-to-negative effect for FICO>740.
findings.evidence: Same RD design, Table VI: effect of a $1,000 limit increase on probability of being 60+/90+ days past due within 48 months, by FICO at origination.
findings.numbers: 60+DPD at 48 months: <=660 +1.21pp on 16.5% base [0.25,2.06]; 661-700 +0.86pp; 701-740 +0.68pp; >740 -0.32pp [-0.61,-0.05]. 90+DPD at 48 months: <=660 +1.16pp on 14.5% base; 661-700 +0.80pp; 701-740 +0.74pp; >740 -0.17pp [-0.45,0.07]. Delinquency is measured only on the treated card, not on other cards.
findings.source_title: Agarwal, Chomsisengphet, Mahoney, Stroebel, QJE 2018, Table VI and Figure VIII
findings.direction: mixed (positive sign below 740, zero or protective above 740)

findings.claim: Credit-limit increases raise debt immediately; the marginal propensity to consume out of liquidity is 10-14% on average and much larger near the limit; for the interest-rate response less than half is balance shifting across cards.
findings.evidence: Panel of US credit card accounts, early 2000s; time-series variation in limits and APRs.
findings.numbers: dDebt/dLimit 10-14%; long-run debt elasticity to APR about -1.3; no delinquency response to limit changes is reported.
findings.source_title: Gross and Souleles, Do Liquidity Constraints and Interest Rates Matter for Consumer Behavior? QJE 2002
findings.direction: supports (limits change total borrowing, the precondition for link 2)

findings.claim: Randomized credit-line increases raise spending but produce no detectable change in delinquency.
findings.evidence: Field experiment randomly assigning 45,307 credit lines at a Turkish bank; effects extend to borrowers far from their limit and with liquid buffers.
findings.numbers: MPB 11 cents per dollar in the first quarter, 28 cents by year 3; 'no discernible effects on delinquencies or labor supply'; slight positive extensive-margin effect on big-ticket loans.
findings.source_title: Aydin, Consumption Response to Credit Expansions: Evidence from Experimental Assignment of 45,307 Credit Lines, AER 2022
findings.direction: contradicts (at least for this bank's customers, more credit did not raise default)

findings.claim: Greater consumer-credit supply to fintech borrowers raises borrowing and raises delinquency.
findings.evidence: Field experiment at a Chinese online lender; treated group given more credit.
findings.numbers: Borrowing +CNY 641 per fortnight in the first two fortnights, effects lasting about 16 weeks; treated borrowers +5.7 percentage points probability of loans 60+ days overdue vs control.
findings.source_title: Fu, Li, Liao, Wang, Xiang, Unveiling the Villain: Credit Supply and the Debt Trap, Journal of Empirical Finance 2025 (SSRN 3257731)
findings.direction: supports (positive sign for a subprime-like population)

findings.claim: Less available credit on credit cards pushes distressed borrowers to default on the mortgage instead of the card; the effect is roughly double the house-price effect and more than 3x larger for low-score than high-score borrowers. In absolute terms less liquidity raises delinquency on both products.
findings.evidence: TransUnion individual panel June 2006 to Dec 2007; cross-sectional regressions of delinquency choice on available cash-equivalent credit and local house prices; not an exogenous-shock design.
findings.numbers: One-SD reduction in available credit: +25% in probability of choosing mortgage over card delinquency; one-SD house-price fall: 13%. Low-credit-quality available-credit coefficient >3x that of high-quality. People delinquent on mortgage while current on cards +127% Jun 2006 to Dec 2007. Aggregate: more available credit -> fewer delinquencies of both types.
findings.source_title: Cohen-Cole and Morse, Your House or Your Credit Card, Which Would You Choose? Boston Fed QAU WP 09-5
findings.direction: supports (cross-product liquidity channel, strongest for low scores)

findings.claim: Illiquidity measured by card utilization across all cards raises mortgage default by as much as negative equity, and the effect is present even with low CLTV.
findings.evidence: Loan-level mortgage data merged with credit bureau records, 2005-06 originations; hazard model.
findings.numbers: High utilization (>80%) raises default hazard by 0.65pp per quarter at CLTV<50, peaking at 1.5pp/q near CLTV 100; CLTV <50 to >120 raises default by 1.3pp/q; county unemployment shocks matter less than high utilization.
findings.source_title: Elul, Souleles, Chomsisengphet, Glennon, Hunt, What 'Triggers' Mortgage Default? AER P&P 2010 (Philly Fed WP 10-13)

findings.claim: The pecking order between mortgage and card default shifted from strongly mortgage-first to indifferent during 2008, and 'illiquidity in the form of available credit' is one of the named drivers.
findings.evidence: OCC nonprime mortgage borrowers 2001-09 linked to card data; the coefficient on available credit was not retrievable (paywalled).
findings.numbers: Pre-crisis consumers were 8x more likely to prioritize mortgage over card; by late 2008 equally likely to default on either.
findings.source_title: Andersson, Chomsisengphet, Glennon, Li, The Changing Pecking Order of Consumer Defaults, JMCB 2013
findings.direction: supports (available credit shifts the entry order)

findings.claim: After a credit-line decrease, prime and above borrowers restore total card balances within three quarters via other cards or new accounts; subprime and deep-subprime borrowers cannot. The report does not measure subsequent delinquency on other accounts.
findings.evidence: CFPB Consumer Credit Panel, CLDs on highest-balance card in 2019Q1, descriptive medians by score tier.
findings.numbers: Median 75% of open line cut; subprime available credit $737 -> $228; prime total available card credit $6,155 -> $3,092; affected-card utilization 94% for prime and below, 37% -> 78% for superprime; median score change after CLD for those with a recent delinquency: -7 (subprime) to -90 (prime) points; without recent delinquency scores recover to near pre-CLD, net -4 to -12 points; CLDs 4x more likely after a recent card delinquency (1.33% vs 0.31%).
findings.source_title: CFPB, Credit Card Line Decreases, June 2022
findings.direction: mixed (prime borrowers substitute across lenders, so a single lender's line matters little to them; subprime borrowers cannot)

findings.claim: The volume of the 'other lenders' lines' channel is concentrated at low FICO: bank-initiated limit increases target revolvers and support most subprime revolving debt; no causal delinquency estimate is given.
findings.evidence: FR Y-14M account-level data 2014-2024 from large US banks; descriptive plus event-study on utilization.
findings.numbers: 12% of cards get an increase each year (~$160bn), ~80% bank-initiated; subprime limits $700 at origination -> $2,700 by year 5 (+285%), superprime $12,000 -> $15,000 (+25%); 4% of revolvers vs 2% of transactors get a bank-initiated increase per quarter; ~30% of each increase becomes new revolving balance; share of revolving balances supported by increases: 60% subprime, 35% near-prime, 20% prime, 12% superprime; about a third of accounts that ever go 30+ DPD do so within 6 months of origination.
findings.source_title: Bord, Kovacs, Moran, Automated Credit Limit Increases and Consumer Welfare, FEDS 2025-088 (and FEDS Note 'More Credit, More Debt', Jan 16 2026)
findings.direction: supports (magnitude of the channel is large below prime, small above)

findings.claim: A negative lender label on the credit file (UK high-cost loan) lowers the score without any change in repayment, causes rationing by standard lenders, and raises default a year later; where the score does not move (the RD marginal applicant), neither rationing nor extra default follows.
findings.evidence: UK storefront high-cost lender, ~50,000 applicants matched to a credit bureau; IV via quasi-random loan-officer leniency and RD at the score cutoff.
findings.numbers: Take-up cuts credit score 4.7% in the application quarter and 10% four quarters later (2SLS); same-quarter default -11% (n.s.), debt-collection searches -16%; default higher at four quarters (significant on county court judgments); non-short-term credit search up by at least one application at quarters 3-4; approval probability jumps ~25pp at the cutoff.
findings.source_title: Liberman, Paravisini, Pathania, High-Cost Debt and Perceived Creditworthiness: Evidence from the UK, JFE 2021 (2016 WP hosted by CFPB)
findings.direction: supports (other lenders read the label and change supply; repayment then changes)

findings.claim: Removing a bankruptcy flag raises scores and other lenders' card limits by about half within three years; the flag itself predicts card delinquency conditional on score, but the paper does not estimate the delinquency consequence of the extra credit.
findings.evidence: Difference-in-differences comparing Chapter 13 filers (flag removed at 7 years) to Chapter 7 filers (10 years), credit bureau panel.
findings.numbers: Score +~10 points (implied default probability -3pp on 32%); card limits +$1,510 (about +50%) on $3,027; balances +$800 (+40%) on $1,911; balance/limit ratio 53%. Hidden flag: +6.4pp card delinquency over 3 years on a 19.3% base, +10.8pp mortgage delinquency on 11.7%.
findings.source_title: Dobbie, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Mahoney, Song, Bad Credit, No Problem? Journal of Finance 2020 (NY Fed Staff Report 795)
findings.direction: supports (label -> other lenders' lines step is large; repayment step unmeasured)

findings.claim: Bankruptcy flag removal roughly doubles credit lines for medium and high-score post-bankruptcy consumers; the widely cited follow-on result that the newly extended borrowers defaulted more was NOT verified in this sweep.
findings.evidence: Musto 2004 using credit bureau panel around 10-year flag removal; numbers taken from a secondary summary, not the paper.
findings.numbers: Reported average lines about $800 -> $2,810 and about $2,000 -> $4,578 in the removal year (secondary source; treat as approximate).
findings.source_title: Musto, What Happens When Information Leaves a Market? Evidence from Postbankruptcy Consumers, Journal of Business 2004

findings.claim: Shorter retention of an arrears flag in Sweden made banks tighten, yet affected borrowers got more net credit and defaulted more often; total defaults did not rise.
findings.evidence: Policy change in Swedish credit-bureau retention (Oct 2003), diff-in-diff.
findings.numbers: Retention fell from ~3.5 years average to exactly 3 years; qualitative direction only in the abstract.
findings.source_title: Bos and Nakamura, Should Defaults Be Forgotten? Philly Fed WP 14-21

findings.claim: A forced increase in minimum payments (a liquidity shock on one card) raises delinquency on that card and shrinks credit access on new cards; the authors note their estimates can be affected by spillovers from other cards the consumer holds.
findings.evidence: Quebec Bill 134 (2019) vs rest of Canada, diff-in-diff on TransUnion Canada credit-report data.
findings.numbers: Minimum payment +0.59pp of balance at introduction; revolving debt -$64 (-3.4%) at 6 months, -$109 on historically revolving cards; delinquency +0.105pp matched (+10% on a 1% base) to +0.229pp unmatched (+23%); new cards fewer and with lower limits; new-card cohorts 0.4-0.5pp more delinquent at 6 months; pre-trends make the delinquency result 'less clear-cut'.
findings.source_title: Allen, Boutros, Guttman-Kenney, Credit Card Minimum Payment Restrictions, Bank of Canada SWP 2024-26
findings.direction: supports (payment-terms shocks propagate to delinquency; cross-card spillover acknowledged, not measured)

findings.claim: Among already-distressed card borrowers, immediate payment reductions (short-run liquidity) produced no improvement; only delayed interest write-downs improved financial and labor outcomes.
findings.evidence: Large field experiment with a US debt-settlement program on distressed credit card borrowers.
findings.numbers: No positive effects of immediate payment reductions; interest write-downs effective despite taking effect 3-5 years later.
findings.source_title: Dobbie and Song, Targeted Debt Relief and the Origins of Financial Distress, AER 2020
findings.direction: contradicts (liquidity relief did not move repayment among the distressed)

findings.claim: Credit-limit volatility is larger than income volatility and drives the credit card puzzle, so limits are a first-order liquidity variable.
findings.evidence: Equifax/NY Fed CCP panel estimates of limit changes.
findings.numbers: Credit limit volatility exceeds most income-volatility estimates and varies over the cycle; model explains why ~1/3 of US households hold both card debt and liquid savings.
findings.source_title: Fulford, How Important Is Variability in Consumer Credit Limits? JME 2015

findings.claim: Card balances of maxed-out borrowers transition into delinquency at a rate far above low-utilization balances; utilization is the variable a line change at any lender moves mechanically.
findings.evidence: NY Fed Consumer Credit Panel, balance-weighted transition rates, Q1 2024.
findings.numbers: About one third of maxed-out (90-100% utilization) balances went delinquent in the last year vs less than a quarter pre-pandemic; 0-20% utilization ~1%; 20-60% ~4%. Maxed-out share: 12.3% lowest income quartile vs 5.5% highest; Gen Z 15.3% vs boomers 4.8%.
findings.source_title: NY Fed Liberty Street Economics, Delinquency Is Increasingly in the Cards for Maxed-Out Borrowers, May 2024

findings.claim: Access to payday credit changes repayment of other obligations, with conflicting signs across studies.
findings.evidence: Melzer 2011 QJE (geographic access), Skiba-Tobacman (RD at approval cutoff, Texas), Morse 2011 JFE (disaster shocks).
findings.numbers: Melzer: difficulty paying mortgage/rent/utility bills +25% among lower-income households with access; Skiba-Tobacman: marginally approved applicants more likely to file bankruptcy; Morse: communities with payday offices had fewer foreclosures after earthquakes.
findings.source_title: Melzer, The Real Costs of Credit Access: Evidence from the Payday Lending Market, QJE 2011 (plus Skiba-Tobacman and Morse 2011)

findings.claim: About 29% of accounts pay at or near the minimum and 9-20% anchor to the minimum; these liquidity-constrained payers are the population in which extra credit elsewhere would change repayment, but the paper does not test link 2.
findings.evidence: One quarter of the US general-purpose card market; changes in issuers' minimum-payment formulas.
findings.numbers: 29% near-minimum payers; 9-20% lower bound on anchoring; CARD Act disclosures moved <1% of accounts.
findings.source_title: Keys and Wang, Minimum Payments and Debt Paydown in Consumer Credit Cards, JFE 2019 (NBER w22742)

gaps: No paper found that estimates delinquency on card B caused by an exogenous credit-limit change at lender A (the exact link-2 object). ACMS observe total balances across all cards but report delinquency only on the treated card; Aydin and Fu et al. report delinquency at the treating lender only.

No causal evidence on the effect of a POSITIVE lender label (an Amex, Chase or other prime tradeline appearing on the file) on other lenders' lines or scores. Every label study found uses a negative label: payday loan (Liberman et al.), bankruptcy flag (Dobbie et al., Musto), arrears flag (Bos-Nakamura). Whether other issuers' models give a premium to a prime-brand tradeline is unknown.

Andersson et al. 2013: the coefficient on available credit in the pecking-order regressions could not be retrieved (Wiley and SSRN returned 403); only the abstract's qualitative statement is confirmed.

Musto 2004: the often-cited result that consumers who received the most new credit after flag removal later defaulted more was not verified from the paper; only line-size numbers from a secondary source were found.

Bord-Kovacs-Moran (FEDS 2025-088) and the CFPB 2022 line-decrease report contain no causal estimate of delinquency after a limit increase or decrease, and the CFPB report does not track delinquency on OTHER accounts after a cut.

No causal UK FCA study of unsolicited credit-limit increases on arrears was found; the FCA remedies (2018) were policy documents, and Adams et al. 2022 (Economica) is about repayment nudges. Gathergood-Guttman-Kenney-Stewart-Weber and Antoniou et al. were not re-opened here (task said verify, not re-derive) and do not, as far as found, estimate a cross-card limit shock.
Bank of Canada: the only relevant paper found is on Quebec minimum-payment rules, not on multi-card credit limits; it acknowledges cross-card spillovers but does not measure them.

No study found on prime (>740) borrowers who receive MORE credit elsewhere and then default; ACMS put that effect at roughly zero or slightly negative, so the answer for the Amex-type population rests on one paper's high-FICO bucket plus Aydin's null.
Argus/TransUnion consortium 'full wallet' analyses of same-person cross-issuer repayment are private; nothing public with numbers was found.

2008-09 credit-line cuts: no paper was found that identifies delinquency on other accounts caused by the cuts (CFPB reports the cuts' size, $405bn June 2008-Jan 2010, and Cohen-Cole-Morse cover 2006-07 only).

evidence.summary: Bottom line for LINK 3: no issuer, rating agency, or academic source has ever published a before/after delinquency or loss rate for the SAME accounts across a US co-brand issuer change. Every disclosed number is a portfolio-level effect on the acquirer's blended book, and every one is contaminated by at least one of: purchase accounting (acquired loans carried at fair value, so Citi booked ZERO Costco losses in the first quarter it owned the book and Capital One's charge-off rate FELL 32bp the quarter it added Walmart while its delinquency rate rose), partner loss-sharing (Walmart bore losses worth ~45bp of Capital One's whole domestic card charge-off rate, which works out to roughly 7-8% of the Walmart balances per year by arithmetic on disclosed figures), re-underwriting at conversion (myFICO confirms the new issuer may reset the credit limit, which is itself the liquidity channel the user is worried about), product change (Costco Visa accepted any Visa, so the card lost its must-have status), and selection at transfer (Costco Canada 2015 moved no accounts at all). Trust-pool facts: Amex removed Costco receivables from the Lending Trust and added $3.0B of other accounts (Amex July 2016 deck); Citi made no lump addition to its master trust between Oct 2014 and June 24, 2017, so Costco accounts were NOT in the Citi trust through at least mid-2017 and its 2016 trust net loss rate (2.50% vs 2.51% in 2015) is unaffected; whether the June 2017 $4.0B addition included Costco is unknown. The strongest evidence for the free-riding mechanism itself is not a US case: Foley-Hurtado-Liberman-Sepulveda (Chile) show that when a retailer's card portfolio was sold to a bank in May 2015, OTHER banks raised those borrowers' limits by ~6.7% within three quarters and the lender raised its own limits 30%, with only a modest, trend-consistent rise in default - direct evidence that a change in how a tradeline is labeled/reported moves other lenders' lines. But the Chile mechanism is an information-regime change (positive data became visible), not a brand halo, so it is an upper bound on what a US badge switch could do. Verdict: the badge-transfer natural experiments exist (Costco ~$10.6B, Walmart $8.1B, Hilton ~$0.5-1.2B, JetBlue, Fidelity $1.7B, Apple Card $20B pending, Discover $98B pending any rebrand) but none has usable public outcome data; the user's third channel is (a) logically real, (b) supported by one non-US quasi-experiment with numbers, and (c) unmeasured for any US issuer switch.

findings.claim: Citi booked zero net credit losses on the acquired Costco portfolio in its first full quarter of ownership (Q3 2016) and told investors to expect 'normalization of losses in the Costco portfolio' - so the acquirer's early loss data say nothing about the transferred borrowers' behavior.
findings.evidence: Citi 3Q16 10-Q (Citi-hosted PDF), North America GCB section: 'In Citi-branded cards, net credit losses increased 1% to $448 million, despite a 24% increase in average loans, as the Costco portfolio did not incur losses in the third quarter of 2016. North America GCB expects net credit losses in both cards portfolios to increase in the near term due to portfolio growth and seasoning, the normalization of losses in the Costco portfolio and the newly proposed regulatory guidelines [on third-party collections].' Portfolio acquired June 17, 2016 (the 10-Q states the date). By Q1 2017 Citi-branded cards NCLs were +31% to $611M 'primarily due to the Costco portfolio acquisition, organic volume growth and seasoning' (Citi Q1 2017 release). No Costco-specific loss rate was ever disclosed.
findings.numbers: Branded-card NCL +1% to $448M on +24% average loans (Q3 2016); Costco losses = 0 that quarter; Q1 2017 branded NCL +31% to $611M; Citi 3Q16 reserve build $408M in NA GCB 'driven by the impact of the acquisition of the Costco portfolio'.
findings.source_title: Citigroup Form 10-Q for Q3 2016 (citigroup.com copy) and Citi First Quarter 2017 Results

findings.claim: Capital One's reported domestic card charge-off rate FELL when it added the Walmart book (Q4 2019) while the 30+ delinquency rate ROSE, because partner loss-sharing suppresses charge-offs but not delinquency - the two metrics moved in opposite directions on the same accounts.
findings.evidence: Q4 2019 earnings call: 'The charge-off rate for the quarter was 4.32%, a 32 basis point improvement year-over-year, driven by the addition of the acquired Walmart portfolio.' and 'Because the delinquency rate is not affected by the loss-sharing agreement, the addition of the Walmart portfolio put upward pressure on the fourth quarter 30-plus delinquency rate.' Fairbank also called the Walmart back book 'a run-off portfolio that's running off at a pretty sizable clip' with 'the loss rate that it has'; CFO disclosed an $84M allowance build for the acquired book. Search snippets of the 2019 10-K (sec.gov, not opened) add: Walmart raised the 30+ DQ rate by 17bp at 12/31/2019 and was expected to cut the 2020 NCO rate by ~25bp.
findings.numbers: NCO 4.32% (-32bp yoy) with Walmart; 30+ DQ 3.93% despite upward pressure; $84M Walmart allowance build; acquired balance ~$8.1B on Oct 11, 2019.
findings.source_title: Capital One Q4 2019 Earnings Call Transcript (Motley Fool)

findings.claim: The Walmart loss-share was large: removing it would have raised Capital One's entire domestic card charge-off rate by ~45bp and its allowance by ~$850M. By arithmetic (not disclosed by the company), Walmart was absorbing losses equal to roughly 7-8% of the Walmart balances per year, and ~10% of balance in lifetime allowance terms.
findings.evidence: Capital One 8-K May 24, 2024 (reported by Payments Dive): without loss sharing the Q1 2024 domestic card NCO rate 'would have been approximately 45 basis points higher' and the allowance 'approximately $850 million higher'; retained portfolio $8.5B, ~40% of it originated by Capital One. Arithmetic: Q1 2024 domestic card average loans $142,887M (Q1 2024 earnings presentation) x 0.0045 = ~$643M annualized; / $8,500M = ~7.6% of Walmart balances borne by Walmart. $850M / $8.5B = 10.0%. The loss-share percentage itself was never disclosed, so the Walmart book's total loss rate is unknown (7.6% / Walmart's share).
findings.numbers: 45bp on ~$143B = ~$643M/yr = ~7.6% of $8.5B; allowance +$826-850M (=~10% of balance); Q2 2024 earnings hit $853M.
findings.source_title: Walmart and Capital One break up (Payments Dive) and Capital One Q1 2024 Earnings Release Presentation

findings.claim: Synchrony's own disclosures show the Walmart book was a high-loss portfolio BEFORE transfer: excluding Walmart and PayPal, Synchrony's charge-off rate was 20-30bp lower year over year, and Fairbank said on the record the Walmart portfolio 'has got high credit losses'. So the drop in Capital One's reported NCO on acquisition is pure accounting/loss-share, not borrower behavior.
findings.evidence: Synchrony Q3 2019 release: NCO 5.35% of average receivables; 'excluding the PayPal Credit program and the Walmart portfolio, the rate decreased approximately 20 basis points'; 30+ DQ 4.47%, flat ex-Walmart/PayPal; $326M pre-tax reserve reduction on the Walmart sale (completed Oct 11, 2019). American Banker: Walmart portfolio ~$10B, ~13% of Synchrony receivables; Fairbank quote; Walmart's lawsuit alleged Synchrony underwrote in a way 'likely to have higher-than-normal losses'.
findings.numbers: SYF NCO 5.35% (Q3 2019), -20bp yoy ex-Walmart/PayPal; Q1 2019 6.06%, -30bp ex; reserve release $326M pre-tax; portfolio ~$10B / 13% of receivables.
findings.source_title: Synchrony Financial Reports Third Quarter 2019 Net Earnings; American Banker 'Loans sold, partnership renewed, lawsuit dropped'

findings.claim: Amex's side of the Costco transfer gives no usable loss number either: Costco and JetBlue loans were moved to held-for-sale on Dec 1, 2015, after which Amex 'does not reflect the associated credit costs', and the company attributed its 2016 write-off rise to 'lending growth initiatives', not to losing low-loss Costco borrowers.
findings.evidence: Amex 2016 Annual Report: 'Card Member loans provision for losses increased $45 million or 4 percent in 2016... primarily driven by strong momentum in our lending growth initiatives, resulting in higher loan balances, increased net write-offs in the current year and a slight increase in delinquencies, partially offset by the impact of the HFS portfolios, as the current year does not reflect the associated credit costs.' Card Member loans net write-off rate (principal only) 1.6% in 2016 vs 1.4% in 2015 vs 1.5% in 2014. Amex July 2016 fixed-income deck: worldwide lending NWO 1.4% (Q2'15) to 1.5% (Q2'16), 30+ DPD 1.0% to 1.1%; Costco U.S. loans HFI were $14.3-15.8B per quarter in 2015 before reclassification. No ex-Costco vs Costco write-off split was ever published.
findings.numbers: NWO principal-only 1.6% (2016) / 1.4% (2015) / 1.5% (2014); Costco US loans ~$14-16B (2015); gain on HFS sales $1.2B (AR) / $1.1B Costco.
findings.source_title: 2016 American Express Company Annual Report (q4cdn PDF)

findings.claim: Amex Credit Account Master Trust pool composition DID change at the Costco sale: Costco co-branded receivables were removed and $3.0B of receivables in additional accounts were added, so the trust's 2016 series break is a mix shift, not a behavior shift.
findings.evidence: Amex Fixed Income Investor Presentation, July 21, 2016, ABS Update slide: 'As a result of the Costco portfolio sale, we took a number of actions: Costco co-branded receivables were removed. The Lending Trust added $3.0B of receivables in additional accounts. The Lending Trust issued two series of investor certificates to provide credit enhancement to certain outstanding series.' Trust size at 6/30/16: principal receivables $24.7B, investor interest $13.0B, seller interest $11.7B (source cited on slide: 10-D dated July 15, 2016). The dollar amount of Costco receivables removed and the removal date are only in the sec.gov 10-D/8-K (not opened).
findings.numbers: Additions $3.0B; trust principal AR $24.7B; investor interest $13.0B; seller interest $11.7B (6/30/16).
findings.source_title: American Express Company Fixed Income Investor Presentation July 21, 2016

findings.claim: Citi's master trust did NOT receive the Costco accounts at the transfer: the prospectus lump-addition table shows no additions between Oct 25, 2014 and June 24, 2017, and the trust's 2016 net loss rate was flat (2.50% vs 2.51%). Whether the June 24, 2017 addition ($4.04B principal, 10.14% of pool) contained Costco accounts is not stated anywhere.
findings.evidence: CCCIT 2017-A5 prospectus (Apr 25, 2017), Annex I: last lump addition Oct 25, 2014 ($1.50B principal); loss table: net losses 2.50% (2016), 2.51% (2015), 2.38% (2014); 30+ delinquency total 3.25% (Dec 2016) vs 3.36% (2015) vs 3.45% (2014). CCCIT 2023-A2 prospectus adds June 24, 2017 lump addition $4,044,377,672 principal = 10.14% of outstanding principal receivables, with no description of the accounts; the string 'Costco' does not appear in either prospectus. Same 2023 table shows the Jan 20, 2018 lump removal of $506,499,529 principal, which matches the Hilton portfolio sale to Amex.
findings.source_title: Citibank Credit Card Issuance Trust prospectuses (2017-A5 and 2023-A2), citigroup.com

findings.claim: At the Costco Amex-to-Citi migration the tradeline kept its open date and payment history but the creditor changed and the credit limit could be reset - so the badge switch was visible to every other lender's model on the same day for ~11M accounts, and the new issuer's limit reset is itself the liquidity shock the user's third channel describes.
findings.evidence: myFICO blog on the transition: 'the account number will change from an Amex to Visa', 'the account date opened and payment history should remain the same', 'there may be a change in the credit limit which may result in a change in credit utilization', 'the migration should not result in a hard inquiry'. myFICO forum threads report Citi was not lenient in underwriting the converted card. Costco accepted any Visa after the switch (View From The Wing), so the card also lost its exclusive-acceptance status - a priority-channel confound.
findings.numbers: No numbers on limit changes were published; Costco US portfolio ~$10.6B, ~11M accounts (Citi/press).
findings.source_title: What does the Costco transition from Amex to Citibank Visa mean to your FICO Score? (myFICO)

findings.claim: Direct quasi-experimental evidence that changing who reports a card account moves OTHER lenders' credit lines: when a large Chilean retailer's card portfolio was sold to a bank (May 2015), other banks raised those borrowers' limits by ~6.7% within three quarters, the lender raised its own limits ~30%, and default rose only modestly with no break in trend.
findings.evidence: Foley, Hurtado, Liberman, Sepulveda, 'The Effects of Information on Credit Market Competition: Evidence from Credit Cards' (working paper; AEA 2019, SSRN 5550904/3550904). Regulator (SBIF) data, 849,449 individuals, 23 lenders; average limit ~$2,800, 90+ default rate 2.2%. Diff-in-diff vs other retail-card borrowers: bank-issued limits for the Lender's borrowers rose 156,000 pesos (~$310), 6.7% of the 2.3M-peso pre-mean, three quarters after the sale; the Lender raised its own limits ~260,000 pesos (30%) by quarter 1; usage and default show 'a modest increase in the propensity to default but no break in trend'. Mechanism: before the sale only defaults were visible to other lenders; after it, limits and usage became visible - an information-regime change, not a brand-halo change. The paper does not test payment hierarchy across cards.
findings.numbers: +156,000 CLP (+6.7%) other-bank limits; +260,000 CLP (+30%) own limits; bank card count +~30%; 90+ default base rate 2.2%.
findings.source_title: The Effects of Information on Credit Market Competition: Evidence from Credit Cards (Foley, Hurtado, Liberman, Sepulveda)

findings.claim: Brazil evidence on the same mechanism: when positive credit information on a group of borrowers became visible to all lenders (SCR threshold cut), their cost of credit fell sharply and loan sizes rose, driven by smaller banks - other lenders act on newly visible tradeline information.
findings.evidence: Bonomo et al., 'Effects of sharing public positive credit information on personal loans' (CEMLA 2021): after the threshold change the cost of credit for affected borrowers fell by 33.5 percentage points and new loan size increased; maturity unchanged; effect concentrated in smaller banks. Does not study delinquency across cards.
findings.numbers: -33.5 pp cost of credit; loan size up (magnitude not captured in the summary).
findings.source_title: Effects of sharing public positive credit information on personal loans (Bonomo et al., CEMLA)

findings.claim: Apple Card (Goldman to JPMorgan, announced Jan 7, 2026, ~24-month transition) is the largest pending badge-switch experiment, and its pre-transfer numbers are unusually well documented: Goldman's card loss rate was roughly double Chase's at a subprime share similar to Capital One's.
findings.evidence: CNBC Sept 2022 (JPMorgan analyst note, regulatory filings): Q2 2022 net charge-off rates Goldman 2.93%, Capital One 2.26%, BofA 1.60%, JPMorgan 1.47%; sub-660 share Goldman 28%, Capital One 30%, JPMorgan 12%. 2026 reporting (9to5mac citing WSJ): Apple Card subprime 34% vs Chase 15% vs Capital One 31%; delinquency ~4% vs 3.05% industry; Goldman was 'less aggressive (and less successful) at recovering charge-off debt'. Deal: ~$20B balances, discount >$1B, JPMorgan $2.2B Q4 2025 provision, Goldman $2.5B reserve release (American Banker). No post-transfer data exist yet; JPMorgan's re-underwriting/line plans are undisclosed. CFO Barnum: 'we are not strangers to subprime'.
findings.source_title: Goldman's Apple Card business has a surprising subprime problem (CNBC via NBC New York); Chase explains why it won't lose billions on Apple Card (9to5mac)

findings.claim: Discover to Capital One (closed May 18, 2025) is not yet a badge-switch test - accounts keep the Discover brand - but the disclosures illustrate the purchase-accounting confound at scale: $19.4B of acquired Discover loans that were already charged off are excluded from Capital One's charge-off rate, and management says Discover 'has historically had lower losses and delinquencies than Capital One'.
findings.evidence: Capital One Q2 2025 call: combined domestic card NCO 5.25% (-80bp yoy) vs legacy Capital One 5.5% (-55bp yoy); 'These metrics were impacted by the addition of Discover, which has historically had lower losses and delinquencies than Capital One'; delinquency metric 'impacted by aligning methodologies'. Acquired $98.3B domestic card loans at a $220M net fair value discount; $8.8B initial allowance on non-PCD loans; $19.4B of fully charged-off Discover loans excluded with $3.3B expected recoveries. Discover's last standalone quarter (Q1 2025): card NCO 5.47%, 30+ DQ 3.66%.
findings.numbers: Combined 5.25% vs legacy 5.5% (Q2 2025); Discover standalone NCO 5.47%, DQ 3.66% (Q1 2025); $98.3B loans; $19.4B charged-off loans excluded.
findings.source_title: Capital One (COF) Q2 2025 Earnings Call Transcript (Motley Fool); Discover Q1 2025 results (BusinessWire)

findings.claim: Cabela's to Capital One (Sept 25, 2017, $5.7B) is a cleaner-looking case because there was no loss-sharing, yet still only blended numbers exist: the store card's 2016 charge-off rate was 2.35% vs Capital One's 4.16%, and Capital One guided the acquisition would cut its NCO rate ~25bp and DQ ~15bp - again a mix effect, not a same-account before/after.
findings.evidence: Forbes/Trefis pre-close analysis: Cabela's 2016 charge-off 2.35% vs Capital One domestic card 4.16%. Capital One Q3 2017 10-Q (via search snippet): ex-Cabela's domestic card NCO would have been 4.66% for Q3 2017; expected reduction ~25bp NCO / ~15bp 30+ DQ going forward. Confounds: fair-value accounting on acquired loans, initial allowance build.
findings.numbers: 2.35% vs 4.16% (2016); guidance -25bp NCO, -15bp DQ; $5.7B added.
findings.source_title: Capital One May Be Able To Acquire Cabela's Card Portfolio After All (Forbes/Trefis)

findings.claim: Costco Canada (CIBC from Capital One, March 4, 2022) discloses price and initial reserve but no delinquency or loss data for the transferred accounts.
findings.evidence: CIBC Q2 2022 report: acquired the Canadian Costco portfolio with $2.9B outstanding for $3.1B cash; recorded $106M pre-tax ($77M after-tax) of acquisition, integration, purchase-accounting and performing-loan provision items; the provision component was $94M for the stage-1 ECL established at acquisition plus stage-1 to stage-2 migration in the quarter. Accounted for as an asset acquisition. No write-off rate for the book was published.
findings.numbers: $2.9B balance; C$3.1B price; $94M performing-loan provision; $106M total pre-tax.
findings.source_title: CIBC Announces Second Quarter 2022 Results

findings.claim: Costco Canada 2015 (Amex to Capital One) is NOT a same-account experiment: Capital One did not buy the Amex portfolio; Amex TrueEarnings holders were moved to Amex SimplyCash and had to apply fresh for the Capital One Costco Mastercard. Sam's Club is also not an experiment: GE Capital Retail Bank simply renamed itself Synchrony (June 2014) and has issued the program for 30+ years.
findings.evidence: Globe and Mail / CBC / CreditCardsCanada coverage of the Jan 1, 2015 switch: new Capital One card, existing Amex cardholders transitioned to SimplyCash. Synchrony newsroom: 30-year Sam's Club relationship renewed; GE Capital Retail Bank became Synchrony Bank June 2, 2014.
findings.numbers: None applicable.
findings.source_title: Costco Canada switches to MasterCard from AmEx (Globe and Mail); Synchrony renews 30-year relationship with Sam's Club

findings.claim: Hilton (Citi to Amex, Jan 30, 2018), JetBlue (Amex to Barclays, sale completed March 18, 2016) and Fidelity (FIA/BofA to Elan/US Bank, 2016, ~$1.7B) are documented transfers with no public loss or delinquency outcome for the transferred accounts; the only quantified trace is Citi's trust removal of 349,952 Hilton accounts / $506.5M principal.
findings.evidence: Citi trust: Jan 20, 2018 lump removal $506,499,529 principal (2023-A2 prospectus table; sec.gov 8-K snippet gives 349,952 accounts and ties it to the Hilton sale); Citi reported ~$1.2B Hilton balances and a ~$150M gain (search snippet, sec.gov 8-K not opened); Amex Q1 2018 10-Q notes the acquired Hilton portfolio. JetBlue: Amex 2016 AR gives the March 18, 2016 completion date; Barclays publishes no US portfolio-level credit metrics. Fidelity: Nilson/CNBC report ~$1.7B balances moved to U.S. Bank's Elan; Amex was network only (cards issued by FIA), so it is an issuer switch BofA-to-US Bank, not Amex-to-anyone.
findings.numbers: Hilton removal $506.5M principal, 349,952 accounts; Fidelity ~$1.7B.
findings.source_title: Fidelity drops credit card partners American Express, Bank of America (CNBC); Citi 2023-A2 prospectus removals table

findings.claim: Logic, not data: even a perfect same-account before/after would not separate brand halo from the third channel, because the transfer simultaneously (1) changes the badge other lenders see, (2) lets the new issuer reset the line, (3) changes the card's usefulness (Costco: exclusive Amex acceptance to any-Visa), (4) changes collections practice (Goldman recovered less than peers; Citi 2016 cited new third-party collection rules), and (5) restarts the charge-off clock via fair-value marks.
findings.evidence: Each element is documented above: myFICO (limit may change), View From The Wing (any Visa accepted at Costco), 9to5mac/WSJ (Goldman less aggressive at recoveries), Citi 3Q16 10-Q (collections guidelines and zero Costco losses), Capital One Q4 2019 call (loss-share suppresses NCO but not DQ). No source attempts to separate these.
findings.numbers: n/a
findings.source_title: Citi Scored the Costco Deal - and Their Card Business Hasn't Recovered (View From The Wing)

gaps: No source of any kind - 10-Q/10-K, earnings call, rating agency, academic - reports delinquency or loss rates for the SAME accounts before and after a US co-brand issuer change (Costco, Walmart, JetBlue, Hilton, Fidelity). Every disclosed number is a blended-portfolio effect on the acquirer.
Walmart/Capital One loss-share percentage was never disclosed, so the Walmart book's gross loss rate cannot be backed out (only Walmart's absorbed share, ~7.6% of balance per year by arithmetic).
Citi never published a Costco-portfolio net credit loss rate; Citi's 2016 10-K and 3Q16 10-Q give only narrative ('did not incur losses', 'normalization of losses').
Amex never published Costco vs ex-Costco write-off rates; the 2016 AR and July 2016 deck only note that HFS credit costs were excluded from Dec 1, 2015.

Amex Lending Trust: the dollar amount and date of the Costco receivables removal and the profile of the $3.0B added accounts are in the July 2016 10-D/8-K on sec.gov (blocked); Fitch/Moody's/S&P commentary on the removal was not found on the open web (paywalled).

Citi trust: whether the June 24, 2017 lump addition ($4.04B principal, 10.14% of pool) included Costco accounts is not stated in the 2017-A7 or 2023-A2 prospectus; static-pool tables are by origination year only, so it cannot be inferred.
Barclays JetBlue portfolio: no size, price, or performance data found anywhere (Barclays PLC does not break out US partner books).

Hilton (Citi to Amex 2018): no post-transfer performance; only Citi's trust removal ($506.5M principal, 349,952 accounts - the account count comes from a sec.gov 8-K search snippet that was not opened).
Apple Card: transfer not executed (24-month transition from Jan 2026); no post-transfer data; JPMorgan's plans for re-underwriting, line cuts, or collections on the ~$20B book are undisclosed.

Discover: no announced rebranding of Discover accounts to Capital One, so no badge-switch test exists yet; Capital One Q1 2025 standalone domestic card NCO was not fetched for a like-for-like comparison with Discover's 5.47%.

No academic paper uses any US portfolio transfer as a natural experiment for delinquency or payment hierarchy. The closest quasi-experiment (Foley-Hurtado-Liberman-Sepulveda, Chile) identifies an information-regime effect on other lenders' limits, not a brand-halo effect, and does not test cross-card payment ordering; it is a working paper (SSRN 3550904), publication status unknown.
CIBC Costco: no delinquency or write-off disclosure for the acquired book beyond the $94M stage-1 provision.

Could not open several primary sources due to blocks or paywalls: Capital One 8-K May 24, 2024 (investor site timed out twice; numbers taken from Payments Dive/American Banker), Seeking Alpha Citi Q3 2016 transcript (403), CNBC original (403; used NBC New York syndication), Alphastreet transcript (403), ped30 (paywall).

evidence.summary:
Bottom line: no public dataset carries lender IDENTITY on tradelines together with a score and a repayment outcome. Bureau research panels that do (NY Fed/Equifax CCP, CFPB CCP, UC-CCP/Experian, Chicago Booth/TransUnion, OSU and UIUC Experian panels) carry at most 'subscriber-based fields' or a 'de-identified lender key' and are restricted (Fed co-author + Fed servers; UC affiliation + $8,240; CFPB staff). The UK FCA multi-card panel behind Gathergood et al. and Antoniou et al. is the only same-person cross-issuer card data with outcomes, and it is not shareable. Argus/TransUnion 'full wallet' is a private consortium product.

What IS testable with public or free-login data, ranked: (1) Home Credit Default Risk (Kaggle, free login) is the best public analog: other lenders' tradelines with CREDIT_TYPE (16 types incl. 'Microloan', 'Credit card', 'Consumer credit'), other-lender credit-card limits (AMT_CREDIT_SUM_LIMIT), MONTHLY days-past-due at other lenders (bureau_balance STATUS 0-5), three external scores (EXT_SOURCE_1/2/3), and the applicant's own loan outcome (TARGET); 307,511 applicants, 1.72M bureau rows, 27.3M bureau-month rows. It can test 'lender TYPE predicts default beyond score' (the reason-code-06 analog) and 'other-lender limits -> own repayment' conditional on score. It cannot name issuers. (2) Lending Club 2007-2018Q4 is a true no-login direct download (DePaul mirror, 1.68 GB) with FICO bands at origination and last pull, other-lender limits by type (total_bc_limit, tot_hi_cred_lim, total_rev_hi_lim, bc_open_to_buy), tradeline counts by lender type (num_bc_tl, num_il_tl, mort_acc, total_cu_tl 'Number of finance trades'), and loan_status; it tests whether bankcard lines granted by other lenders and finance-company trade counts predict LC default within FICO band. (3) NY Fed SCE Credit Access (public Excel microdata, ~1,300/wave, 3 waves/yr since 2013) has self-reported score band, lender-initiated limit cuts, limit-increase requests granted/rejected, maxed-out, and 30+/90+ late; it tests the liquidity -> repayment link within score band but has no issuer. (4) SCF 2022 identifies Amex (code 51), Discover (50), general-purpose (38) and store cards (X7973/X7974/X7976) with 60-day-late (X3005) and turned-down (X407), but no score, cross-section only, and the public file may collapse institution codes. (5) SHED 2025 (public CSV, 12,934) has self-rated score band, applied/denied for cards, and 'did not pay minimum on at least one card' (284 of 10,759) but no issuer. Atlanta Fed DCPC, Philly Fed Y-14M aggregates, Kaggle Amex (anonymized) and Prosper (login) add little to this chain.

Published evidence for the label channel itself: Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania show a UK high-cost loan cuts the average applicant's credit score 4.7% in the quarter of application and ~10% four quarters later, with more default and rationing later, while the marginal applicant (score unaffected) shows no default change; Antoniou et al. (same UK 1.6M-borrower panel) show that after a default on one card, credit limits on the borrower's OTHER cards fall by an average of about £700 and the bureau 'Charged-off rate' rises; FICO reason code 06 'Too many consumer finance company accounts' is confirmed in published FICO reason-code lists. These support the mechanism (other lenders read lender-type/labels beyond score and reprice lines), but none of them measures a positive Amex/Chase badge effect on other lenders' lines; that link remains plausible but unmeasured.

findings.claim: Home Credit Default Risk is the most useful public dataset for the chain: it carries other lenders' tradelines by TYPE, other-lender credit-card limits, monthly days-past-due at other lenders, three external scores, and the applicant's own default outcome.
findings.evidence: Official column dictionary (mirrored on GitHub): bureau.csv CREDIT_TYPE = 'Type of Credit Bureau credit (Car, cash,...)'; AMT_CREDIT_SUM_LIMIT = 'Current credit limit of credit card reported in Credit Bureau'; CREDIT_DAY_OVERDUE, AMT_CREDIT_SUM_OVERDUE, AMT_CREDIT_MAX_OVERDUE; bureau_balance.csv STATUS = 'C closed, X unknown, 0 no DPD, 1 = DPD 1-30, 2 = DPD 31-60, ... 5 = DPD 120+ or sold or written off' by month; application TARGET = '1 - client with payment difficulties: late payment more than X days on at least one of the first Y installments'; EXT_SOURCE_1/2/3 = 'Normalized score from external data source'; credit_card_balance.csv has SK_DPD and AMT_CREDIT_LIMIT_ACTUAL for Home Credit's own cards. CREDIT_TYPE has 16 values incl. Consumer credit, Credit card, Car loan, Mortgage, Microloan, Mobile operator loan, Loan for business development. Concrete test: regress TARGET on count of 'Microloan' tradelines controlling for EXT_SOURCE_1-3 (lender-type signal beyond score, the reason-code-06 analog); second test: among applicants with an active other-lender credit card, regress TARGET on AMT_CREDIT_SUM_LIMIT within EXT_SOURCE bands (other-lender lines -> own repayment). Limits: lender identity not named, only type; bureau history is pre-application; country not stated; needs a free Kaggle account and rule acceptance.
findings.numbers: 307,511 train applicants; bureau.csv 1,716,428 rows; bureau_balance.csv 27,299,925 rows; CREDIT_ACTIVE Closed 1,079,273 / Active 630,607 / Sold 6,527 / Bad debt 21 (https://harnalashok.github.io/credit_risk/bureau.html)

findings.direction: neutral: dataset capability, not evidence for or against

findings.evidence: Questionnaire wording extracted from the PDF: N3 'Over the past 12 months, did you max out (borrow up to the limit) on any of your credit cards?'; N4 options include 'Apply for a credit card' and 'Request an increase in the credit limit of a credit card'; N9 'Was your request for [X] granted?' (Below 620 / 620-679 / 680-719 / 720-760 / Above 760 / Don't know). Page lists 'Complete Microdata' (Excel) as a download. Concrete test: within N22 band, does a lender-initiated limit cut (N14) or a rejected limit increase (N9=3) in wave t predict 30+ late (N15) in wave t+1, using the rotating 12-month panel. Limits: self-reported, ~1,300 per wave, no issuer, no per-card data.

findings.claim: Bureau research panels (NY Fed/Equifax CCP, CFPB CCP, UC-CCP, Chicago Booth TransUnion, OSU/UIUC Experian) hold tradeline-level limits, scores and delinquency but are not public, and per the AEA 2023 credit-data guide they expose at most 'subscriber-based fields' or a 'de-identified lender key', not issuer names.
findings.evidence: NY Fed FAQ: 'Access to the Consumer Credit Panel (CCP) microdata is limited to Federal Reserve System researchers, and their coauthors, due to contractual limitations with the data provider.' Guide slides: key variable types are 'Payment grids ... Statuses ... Subscriber-based fields ... Credit limits ... Balances'; enhancements list 'De-identified lender key'; 'Access to Federal Reserve System credit panels generally requires co-authorship with Fed researcher, requires signing of user agreement and data can only be accessed on FRS servers'; lists UC-CCP (2% national + 100% California, quarterly since 2004), OSU 1% Experian 2019-2020, Chicago 10% TransUnion panel, UIUC Gies 1% Experian. UC-CCP page: eligible = UC faculty/students/employees (non-UC co-authors with approval); basic access $8,240, linkage $12,529, ~6-week review, tradelines include 'loan type, balance amount, minimum payment, credit limit, open and closure dates' and does not say creditor names are included. Concrete test if access obtained: same-person, same-month 30+ entry by lender key across cards, conditional on score and limits, which is the missing hierarchy estimator.
