findings.claim: The UK FCA multi-card panel (Gathergood et al. AER 2019; Antoniou-Lyman-Pagel-Stewart 2025) is the only known same-person, cross-issuer card panel with outcomes, and it directly shows the reverse label channel: a default on one card lowers credit limits on the borrower's other cards by about £700 and raises the bureau 'Charged-off rate'.
findings.evidence: Antoniou et al. text: 'We use a dataset covering more than 1.6 million credit card borrowers over a period of 2 years in the UK [see also Gathergood et al., 2019]. In this sample, (roughly) 356 thousand individuals enter delinquency at some point, with approximately 30 thousand of them having their debt eventually written off.' ... 'defaulting on a card significantly raises a borrower's Charged-off rate for other cards' ... 'credit limits on other cards drop significantly when a default on another card happens' ... 'Credit limits are also lower, by an average of £700'. Average credit limit £4,807.7, APR 22.3%, utilization 74.7%. Data came via FCA statutory powers merged with credit files; the openICPSR replication page for the AER paper returned HTTP 403 in this session, so whether it holds data or only code is unverified. This is evidence that other lenders reprice lines on a label (a default), i.e., the chain label -> other lenders' lines exists in the negative direction; it does not measure a positive Amex/Chase badge effect.
findings.numbers: 1.6M borrowers, 2 years; ~356k enter delinquency; ~30k written off; other-card limits fall ~£700 on average after a default; mean limit £4,807.7
findings.source_title: Opportunistic Borrowing in the Credit Card Market / Do Borrowers Exploit Credit Card Default as Insurance? (Antoniou, Lyman, Pagel, Stewart, Nov 2025)

findings.claim: Liberman-Paravisini-Pathania show a lender-type label on the credit file moves other lenders' decisions beyond repayment behavior: a UK high-cost loan cuts the average applicant's credit score and future bank credit, while the marginal applicant whose score is unaffected shows no change in default or rationing.
findings.evidence: Working paper text: 'taking up a high-cost loan causes an immediate and permanent decline on the credit score, and leads to more default and credit rationing by standard lenders in the future. In contrast, the marginal applicant, whose credit score is not affected, is not more likely to default and does not experience further credit rationing after take-up.' Quantitatively: 'The Lender causes an immediate 4.7% drop in credit scores ... four quarters after ... causally reduced by 10%'; 'receiving a high-cost loan lowers the propensity to be in default by roughly 11%' in the short run with default higher four quarters later; RDD applicants just above the cutoff have '18% to 27% higher probability of receiving a loan' and scores 'not' significantly affected. Published version (JFE 2021, 142(2), 719-736) abstract per FMG/ScienceDirect: high-cost credit reduces credit scores and future bank credit 'even though it does not affect future debt repayment'. Sample: UK high-cost lender, first-time applicants, approval rate 76%, take-up 67%, APR above 700%, 5.3 open tradelines on average. Data not public.
findings.numbers: score -4.7% same quarter, -10% at 4 quarters (average applicant); short-run default -11%; RDD take-up jump ~25pp; JFE 142(2):719-736
findings.source_title: High-Cost Debt and Borrower Reputation / High-cost debt and perceived creditworthiness: Evidence from the UK (Liberman, Paravisini, Pathania)

findings.claim: FICO reason code 06 'Too many consumer finance company accounts' is a documented, score-level penalty on lender TYPE, confirming that the bureau score itself reads lender identity class from tradelines.
findings.evidence: Published FICO reason-code lists show code 06 = 'Too many consumer finance company accounts'; explainer: 'the negative reason code relates to the presence of the accounts', and consumer finance companies are 'distinct from banks, credit unions, and credit card issuers in a specific way that FICO tracks'. This is the same mechanism (lender type as a signal) that the free-riding claim needs; note it is a NEGATIVE label effect, and no published source located in this sweep documents a positive badge (Amex/Chase) effect inside FICO.

gaps: No public dataset was found that names the card ISSUER (Amex, Chase, Synchrony, Capital One) on a person's tradelines together with a credit score and a repayment outcome; every candidate carries lender TYPE at most.

No public same-person, multi-issuer card panel exists; the only one located (UK FCA panel, 1.6M borrowers) is not shareable, and the openICPSR replication page for Gathergood et al. (project 116207) returned HTTP 403 so its contents (code vs data) are unverified.

No published study measuring a POSITIVE badge effect (holding an Amex/Chase card raising other lenders' limits or approval odds conditional on score) was found; Liberman et al. and Antoniou et al. document negative label effects only. This link remains plausible but unmeasured.

Whether the SCF public-use file preserves institution code 51 (American Express) or collapses it with other card issuers is unknown; the codebook warns of 'code collapsing for institution variables for public data set' and the master institution list was not opened.

Home Credit: the country of the data is not stated, the bureau history is pre-application only (no overlap with the Home Credit loan performance window for a true hierarchy test), and no non-Kaggle mirror of bureau.csv/bureau_balance.csv was found (Hugging Face search returned nothing).

CFPB Making Ends Meet PUF codebooks were not opened, so whether linked bureau variables (score band, card count, limits) are in the public file is unknown.
Prosper's help page returned HTTP 403; whether historical listing data can be pulled today without an investor account is unknown.

Experian/Equifax/TransUnion academic panels (UC-CCP, OSU 1%, Chicago Booth 10%, UIUC Gies): none of the sources state whether a lender key (even de-identified) is included in the standard extracts; the guide mentions 'de-identified lender key' only as an optional enhancement.

sim.headline: Refuted in simulation: with ACMS-calibrated liquidity effects, free-riding adds less than 0.01 pp of spurious "brand effect" to pool-level and cross-sectional estimators for prime holders (selection adds -0.31 to -0.49 pp, 100x more), has the wrong sign for a halo when holders include subprime (+0.016 to +0.039 pp, holders look worse), leaves person x month FE estimators immune to the person-level term, and leaves a 0.5-1 pp card-level residue on the hierarchy scale in (d) that pre-spell line/balance controls in (e) remove to within noise.
sim.setup: Monte Carlo in numpy/pandas: N=200,000 people x 12 months x 2-4 cards each from 5 issuers (issuer 0 = premium, base line $12k; others $8k, $5k, $2.5k, $3.5k, scaled by exp(0.8 x standardized FICO + 0.15 x issuer-private signal)). Unobserved creditworthiness theta ~ N(0,1); FICO = 700 + 60 x (0.7 theta + 0.714 noise), clipped 520-850; FICO tiers <=660 / 661-700 / 701-740 / >740 as in Agarwal et al. 2018 (about 25% each). 60% of people apply for the premium card; approval requires FICO >= 680 (the RD cutoff; sensitivity at 620) and, with SELECTION on, a private signal theta + 0.8 noise > 0 (with selection off, a coin with the same approval rate, so premium share is 24% in both). FREE-RIDING multiplies the other issuers' lines by (1 + GAMMA) when the badge is present. LINE ENDOGENEITY: each line = own base + 0.05 x sum of other issuers' lines, two best-response rounds (always on). Balances = utilization x line, utilization 0.60/0.45/0.32/0.15 by tier + noise. Person liquidity Q = sum of room across cards + cash. Delinquency latent index on card j = -0.8 theta + person-month shock N(0,1) - beta(tier) Q/1000 + kappa(tier) total balance/1000 - B1 room_j/1000 + B2 balance share_j - ALPHA x premium_j + card-month noise N(0,1); D = 1[index > tier threshold], thresholds calibrated in the all-off world so monthly 30+ entry is 3.0/1.5/0.7/0.25% by tier. Card-level draws are indexed by issuer slot so counterfactuals (brand off, free-riding off) reuse the same noise. Estimators: (a) premium cards minus non-premium cards, reweighted to premium cards' 10-point FICO mix; (b) LPM of other-card 12-month delinquency on holds-premium with FICO-bin FE; (c) holders only, person FE on card-level 12-month means, premium dummy; (d) holders only, person x month FE on months with >= 1 late and >= 1 current card (the first-to-30+ hierarchy sample), premium dummy; (e) = (d) plus line, balance, room, balance share (pre-spell by construction); (f) fuzzy RD among applicants within 15 FICO points of the cutoff, local linear, outcome = person's other-card delinquency, ITT / first stage. 8 scenarios {free-riding off/on} x {brand 0/0.4} x {selection off/on} at cutoff 680, plus sensitivities (GAMMA 0.25; cutoff 620 with free-riding off/0.10/0.25). 5 seeds; means reported with Monte Carlo se = sd/sqrt(5). Runtime about 12 s per seed. Truth: for (a),(c) the counterfactual brand effect on premium-card monthly 30+ (same draws, ALPHA on vs off); for (b),(f) exactly 0 (the brand term touches only the premium card); for (d),(e), whose scale is 'share of late cards in a mixed month' and not a population pp, the same estimator's value in the clean world (free-riding off, selection off, same brand, same seed), so bias there = what the channels add. Free-riding's true causal effect on holders' other cards is computed by counterfactual and reported in the notes.
sim.parameters: GAMMA (free-riding, other issuers' line response to a premium badge) = 0.10 baseline, 0.25 sensitivity: ASSUMED; no published estimate for a positive brand badge. Bracketed by Foley-Hurtado-Liberman-Sepulveda (Chile): other banks raised limits +156,000 CLP = +6.7% when a retailer's good-standing tradelines became visible (https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2019/preliminary/paper/rsHZaEYz), and Dobbie et al.: bankruptcy-flag removal +$1,510 = +50% in card limits over 3 years (https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr795.pdf). LAM_L (line endogeneity) = 0.05 per $ of other issuers' lines, two rounds: ASSUMED, unpublished for US issuers. JMCB 2013, available credit shifts the pecking order, no coefficient published; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jmcb.12001): ASSUMED. B2 = 0.50 per unit of balance share (Gathergood et al. AER 2019 balance matching; https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faer.20180288): ASSUMED magnitude. caveats: The size of the third channel in this simulation is driven by the ACMS-anchored liquidity/burden coefficients (beta, kappa) and by the assumed GAMMA (0.10/0.25). Because premium holders are at FICO >= 680, they sit in the tiers where ACMS finds near-zero net line effects, so a small effect is built in by the calibration; the result is 'near zero under the only published numbers', not 'near zero in the world'. GAMMA for a positive brand badge has never been measured; the Chile (+6.7%) and bankruptcy-flag (+50%) anchors are for information-regime changes and negative labels.

Sign of the card-level residue in (d) depends on B1 (own-card room) vs B2 (balance share), both assumed. Here B2 dominates so free-riding makes the premium card look MORE protected; the econometrician's prediction (downward bias on measured premium priority via other cards' extra room) would hold if B1 dominated. Nobody has estimated these two jointly.

Estimators (d) and (e) are on the 'share of late cards in a mixed month' scale, not a population pp; their 'true' column is the same estimator's clean-world value with the same seed, so their bias column measures what selection and free-riding add, not distance from a population causal effect. Selection alone shifts them by about -1 pp (se 0.4-0.6) through sample composition, which is estimand heterogeneity rather than confounding.

The simulated line changes are pre-spell by construction; post-spell line cuts (Antoniou et al.: other cards' limits fall about GBP 700 after a default) are not simulated, so (e) is cleaner here than it would be with same-month lines in real data. Lines respond to other lines through two best-response rounds but not to the borrower's distress.

Calibration check: +$1000 on one card's line moves that card's 12-month any-30+ by +2.10/+0.36/-0.02/-0.09 pp by tier vs ACMS +1.16/+0.80/+0.74/-0.17 pp on 90+DPD over 4 years; signs match but the 661-740 tiers are weaker than ACMS, so the positive-sign contamination at cutoff 620 and in the 661-740 band may be understated.

Linear probability models with rank-deficient controls in (e) (room = line - balance) are solved by minimum-norm least squares; the premium coefficient is unaffected but its MC se is 2-4x that of (d) because the premium line is nearly collinear with the premium dummy within person.

The RD (f) is noisy (MC se 0.06-0.15 pp) at N=200,000 with a 15-point bandwidth; its estimand in this DGP includes the premium card's own line as liquidity for the other cards (-0.068 pp in (b) with every channel off at cutoff 680; +0.27 pp at cutoff 620), which is a terms effect, not brand or free-riding.

Single-issuer brand term enters only the premium card's index; a hierarchy in which protecting one card mechanically pushes another card late (min-V ordering) is not modeled, so the estimators' behavior under a true 'substitution' hierarchy is untested.

pubdata.dataset: Lending Club accepted-loan file, 2007-2018Q4 (2,260,701 loans, 151 columns), downloaded without login from the DePaul University econdata mirror (1,675,133,810 bytes; the row count matches the well-known 2007-2018Q4 release). Fields used: fico_range_low/high ('the lower/upper boundary range the borrower's FICO at loan origination belongs to'), total_bc_limit ('Total bankcard high credit/credit limit'), bc_open_to_buy ('Total open to buy on revolving bankcards'), num_bc_tl ('Number of bankcard accounts'), total_cu_tl ('Number of finance trades'), loan_status, term, issue_d, annual_inc, dti, loan_amnt (definitions from the LC data dictionary mirror at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/d-osei/Lending-Club-Loan-Data/master/LCDataDictionary.csv). Because Lending Club is an installment lender, every bankcard limit on the file was set by OTHER lenders (card issuers) before the LC loan existed.
pubdata.method: Sample: term == '36 months', issued Jan 2012 to Dec 2017 (1,233,549 loans), loan_status in {Fully Paid, Charged Off} (950,379; Current/Late/Grace/Default dropped), non-missing FICO and bankcard fields and total_bc_limit > 0 (917,334 final). default = 1 if Charged Off. fico = midpoint of the 4-point FICO band. Regressors: fico; log(total_bc_limit + 1); otb_share = bc_open_to_buy / total_bc_limit clipped to [0,1]; num_bc_tl. All standardized on the training split. Logistic regression fit by Newton-Raphson in numpy (ridge 1e-6 for conditioning), 70/30 random holdout (seed 42; seed 7 as check), AUC by Mann-Whitney rank formula with tie averaging. Models: M1 default ~ fico; M2 default ~ fico + log bc limit + otb_share + num_bc_tl; M3 bankcard fields only (no FICO). Repeated within FICO tiers 660-699, 700-739, 740+. Robustness (separate script): R1 = mature vintages only (2012-2015, every 36-month loan reached maturity before 2018Q4; 560,980 loans) with issue-year dummies; R2 = R1 plus log annual income, dti, log loan amount. Plus tabulations of charge-off rate by other-lender bankcard-limit quintile within FICO tier, and by limit tercile within FICO tier x income tercile. Run via 'cd C:/Users/samwe/code/abs-risk && python -m uv run python <script>'. A prior run of the same scripts existed in the scratch folder from earlier today; I re-ran the main script and confirmed every AUC and coefficient reproduces exactly.

pubdata.interpretation: (b) Supported by these numbers: the total bankcard line that other lenders chose to give a person carries real information about that person's later default beyond FICO, and the information is strongest exactly where FICO says least. In the 740+ tier the bankcard fields alone (AUC 0.61) beat FICO alone (0.56), and a borrower in the top quintile of other-lender lines charges off at 4.7% versus 10.8% in the bottom quintile at the same FICO. The sign is negative everywhere: more line from other lenders means safer. The z-scores (15 to 31) leave no doubt about statistical existence; the economic size is modest overall (AUC +0.005 across all tiers) but large within prime (AUC +0.03 to +0.07). About half of the raw effect is income/wealth proxying (the coefficient barely moves when self-reported income, dti and loan size are added, and the tercile grid shows the gradient inside every income cell), so the residual is either private information those lenders had (their own performance history on the account, internal scores) or unobserved capacity that limits track better than FICO does. This is precisely the 'free-rider signal': a later lender who reads total_bc_limit off the bureau file is borrowing the earlier issuers' judgments, and this test says the borrowed judgment is worth something. (a) By logic: this same result shows why an observational estimate of the user's third channel (lines elsewhere -> liquidity -> repayment) cannot be recovered from cross-sectional data. The causal literature (Agarwal et al. 2018) says a $1,000 exogenous line increase RAISES default for FICO <=660; the observational correlation here says higher lines go with LOWER default in the same FICO range. The gap is selection: lenders give lines to people they judge safe, and their judgment is partly right. So any hierarchy or brand estimator that conditions on FICO but not on other lenders' line decisions will attribute the issuers' selection skill to the borrower's FICO tier, and any estimator that does condition on those lines will be conditioning on an outcome of the very badges it is trying to price. That is the contamination the user suspected, now with a measured size: within prime, other-lender line assignment predicts default about as strongly as FICO itself (standardized -0.34 vs -0.25 at 740+). (c) Plausible but unmeasured here: whether an Amex or Chase tradeline specifically raises other lenders' lines; whether the predictive content of total_bc_limit comes from lender identity or only from lender-agnostic capacity; and which card goes late first (Lending Club is a single installment loan, so this says nothing about hierarchy across cards). Also note the finance-trade count carries the OPPOSITE sign from FICO reason code 06 in this population (z -9.5, small), which means at least in a 660+ installment-loan applicant pool the 'consumer finance company' label does not add adverse information once FICO and bankcard fields are in; the FICO penalty may be selection-corrected already or may not transfer to this population.
